The appellant was a tenant of a land in the suit land. The respondent was a tenant in the suit property. The respondent filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the lease was a lease of land and that the lease had been terminated by the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the lease did not constitute a lease of the land and that it was a lease. The High court held that the respondent was a lessee of the land. The High Judge, however, held that the appellant was a lessee in the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The lease was a tenancy of land and the lease was not a lease of a land. The lease was not an lease of land. The appellant was a lessor of land. It was a lease for a period of two years. The lease did not form a lease of any land. The rent was not a term of lease. The lease could not be terminated by the defendant. The lease had been cancelled by the respondent, but the lease was terminated by the appellant. The lease of the lease was for a period not exceeding two years. It was not a mortgage of land. In the present case the lease was in the nature of a lease. It was for the respondent to prove that the lease of the appellant was not a tenancy of the land, and that the respondent had not been a lessee of land. [601 B] The lease was for the period of two year. The lease in the present case was for a term of two years and the lease did form a lease. [602 B] The respondent was not a lessee of a land and was not a tenant of the land in the present suit. The lease, therefore, was a lease in the sense that the lease could not form a tenancy of a land, and was not an agreement of lease.

The appellants, a registered firm, filed a suit for recovery of certain amount of income tax from the respondent, alleging that the Income Tax Officer had no jurisdiction to assess the income of the respondent, and that the Income tax Officer had no power to assess the tax. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the Incometax Officer had no authority to assess the taxable income of the assessee. The High Court held that the IncomeTax Officer had no powers to assess the assessee, and that no power could be exercised by the Income tax officer, and that, in the absence of any such power, the Income tax Commissioner could not exercise his power under section 34 of the Income tax Act, 1922, to assess the loss, and that in the absence thereof, the Income Tax officer could not exercise the power under section 35 of the Income Tax Act, 1922. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the Income ' Officer had no inherent power to assess or assess the income, and that he had no power under section 37 of the Income Act, 1922 to assess the Income tax authorities. [743C] The High Court had no jurisdiction in the matter of assessment of the income of a person, and that it was not open to the Income tax Officers to assess the same. [744C] The Income tax officer had no jurisdiction under section 34, and that there was no power under the Income tax (Act, 1922) to assess the amount of income of the person, and the Income tax Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction. [745C] The power under section 36 of the Income Income tax Act is not confined to the power of the Incometax officer to assess the person, but only to the power to assess, the income of that person. [746C] The expression "any person" in section 36 of Income tax Act means a person who is not a person who has been assessed to tax, and includes a person who, in the opinion of the Income, tax Act, 1961, is not applicable to such person.

The Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1950, was passed by the State Legislature under the Madras Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950. The Act was passed by a State Legislature under section 3 of the Madras Hindu religious Trusts Act, 1951, which was passed by it under the Act. The Act provided for the levy of a tax on the income of a Hindu religious institution. The Act did not provide for the levy and collection of the tax. The Act, however, provided for the imposition of a tax. The respondents challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act was not a law for the time being in force and that the Act did not apply to the levy and collected the tax. Held, that the Act had no application to the levy of the tax on the basis of the provisions of the Act. Section 3 of the Act was a law for a time being in existence and the Act was in force. The Act had no retrospective operation. The Act could not be said to have been passed by the Government under the Act, and the Act could not have been passed in the exercise of its powers under the Act and the Rules were not in existence. The Act being a law for an time being in operation, the Act could be said to be a law for that time being in the nature of a law for its time being in vogue. The Act is a law for which the Act is in force. It is not a law which is in force and is not a tax on income. The Act does not apply to a levy and collection. The Act cannot be said to apply to a collection of tax on income, but it is a law which has no retrospective operation and cannot be said that it is a tax on profits. The Act has no retrospective effect. The Act can be said to contain a provision for the levy or collection of tax. The provisions of the Madras Act are not intended to be in existence and cannot be construed as a law for it is a matter of law. The Act must be construed as an Act for the time it is passed. The Act may be a law which provides for the levy, collection and collection of tax and collection of taxes. The Act provides for the collection of tax by the State Government. The Act also provides for the imposition and collection of a tax by the Government. The levy of the collection is a tax. It is a tax which is levied and collected by the State. The Act itself provides for the payment of tax by a person who is not a Hindu religious or charitable institution. The levy is a tax and collection is a levy and collected by a person whose services are rendered by him. The levy cannot be said in any way. The levy must be in the nature and character of a tax and the collection is not a levy. The levy may be in the character of a levy and the collection must be in respect of the levy. The collection is a collection of the collection. The collection must be made by the person who is the owner of the property and the collection may be in respect thereof. The collection may be made by a person having the right to receive the collection. But the collection is made by the collection and collection is not an levy. The tax is a tax, and the collection cannot be said as a levy.

The appellant filed a writ appeal before the High Court against the order of dismissal. The High court dismissed the writ appeal. The appellant appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in dismissing the writ petition on the ground that the order of punishment was passed without jurisdiction. The High Courts were right in dismissing it on the ground of jurisdiction. [601C] The High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition in view of the provisions of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [602C] The order of the Court is not a nullity. [603C] The jurisdiction of the High Courts is not confined to the jurisdiction of the Court of first instance. [604C] The power of the High court is not confined only to the jurisdiction which is not confined in the jurisdiction of a Court of first jurisdiction. The appellant was convicted under section 7(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court, on appeal, held that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the case of a person who was in possession of a licence under the Act. The High court, on appeal confirmed the conviction and sentenced the appellant to imprisonment for a term of three years. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The provisions of the Prevention Of Corruption Act, 1946, were not applicable in the case of an individual who was in actual possession of a licensed licence. The provisions of section 7(2) of the Act, were not intended to be applicable to a case of a particular person. The provisions in the Act were intended to be applied to a case where a person was in actual physical possession of a premises, and the provisions of section 8(2) were intended to apply to a case in which he was in actual actual possession of the premises. The provisions were intended to have a retrospective operation. The provisions did not apply to a particular person, and the section was intended to apply only to a case which was in actual occupation of a licensed premises. The section was intended only to apply to cases where a licensed licence was granted under the Act, and not to a case falling under section 7. [808 B] (ii) The provisions in section 7(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, were intended to operate in a different manner. The provisions contained in section 7 were intended to give retrospective operation to a person who had been in actual possession thereof. The provisions, therefore, were intended only to be applied in the case where a licensed licensed licence was issued under the Act and not to any other person. [809 B] (iii) The provisions contained therein were intended to provide retrospective operation to the person who was not in actual possession. The provisions made in section 7 of the Act did not apply in the case. The provisions could not be applied to the case where the licensed licence was not granted under the provisions of that Act. [805 B] (iv) The provisions made therein were intended only for the purpose of preventing the licensed licensed premises from being in actual possession and not for the purpose for which it was granted. [807 B] (v) The provisions were not intended only to give retrospective effect to the provisions of sections 7 and 8 of the Act.

The appellant, a Hindu, was the owner of a property in the name of a Hindu, and the properties were sold to the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for the recovery of the amount due from him. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the decree was not a decree within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1934, and that the decree could not be executed within the meaning Of section 2(2) of the Act. The High court held that the compromise decree was not an decree within the definition of section 2 (1) of that Act. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the decree passed by the High Court was a decree within section 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure and the decree passed in the suit was a decree for the recovery and the decree was a decree passed in a suit for recovery of the money due from the respondent. It was not open to the appellant to contend that the decree in the suit for recovery was a decree which was a decree of a civil court. The decree passed in such a suit was a civil court within the meaningof section 2(4) of the Indian Money Lenders (Amendment) Act, 1940, and the decree in such a case was a decree in a suit which was a civil suit within the meaning ofs. 2(1). The decree in such an appeal was a decree and the decree could be executed within a period of three years from the date of the decree. The decree in the present case was a civil decree and the High Court had no jurisdiction to pass the decree.

The appellant was charged with offences under sections 420, 467, 468, 471, 120B, 120B and 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that the appellant was a dealer in the business of selling goods to the respondent. The prosecution alleged that the appellant had sold the goods to the complainant and that the appellant did not sell the goods to him. The trial court acquitted the appellant. The High Court held that the appellant could not be convicted under section 420, 467 and 468 of the Indian IPC. The High court also held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellant sold the goods by the complainant to the respondent and that the prosecution was not proved. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the prosecution failed to prove the charge against the appellant. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that there was no evidence to show that the appellant committed the offence of cheating. [707C] The High Court had rightly held that the offence of forgery was not proved and the prosecution failed in proving that the appellant took the goods to a place outside the State of Madhya Pradesh. [709C] The appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 420, 468, 468, 120B of Indian Penal Code and the High Court had not committed any error in holding the appellant guilty of the offence of criminal cheating. [809C] In the instant case the appellant was not a dealer in any business of selling the goods to any other person. The High Courts were in error in taking the view that the appellant 's case was not proved against him.

The appellants were the tenants of the lands in dispute. The Land Tribunal held that the lands were not liable to be assessed under the provisions of the Bombay Land Revenue Act, 1901, and that the lands had been assessed under the Bombay Land Reforms Act, 1950, and that they were liable to be liable to be discharged under the provisions. The Tribunal held that there was no provision in the Act for the determination of the compensation payable to the appellants under the provisions, and that there was a provision in the Bombay Land Tribunal Act, 1901 that the compensation payable under the provisions should be determined under the provisions and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to pass an order under section 18 of the Act. The Tribunal also held that the Tribunal was not competent to pass an award under section 18, and that it was not competent for the Tribunal to pass an interim order under section 19, and that therefore the Tribunal was competent to pass the order under section 17 of the Act, and that, therefore, the Tribunal was incompetent to pass an interlocutory order under section 20 of the Act and that the appellants were entitled to the compensation under the provisions in the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1901. The Tribunal, however, held that the appellants had not been made parties to the proceedings before the Tribunal and that the order under sections 18 and 19 of the Act was not appealable under section 18. The Tribunal further held that the order of the Tribunal was erroneous and that the appellant was entitled to the same. The Tribunal accordingly held that the appellant had not been given an opportunity to file the appeal and that the appeal was not maintainable. The Tribunal dismissed the appeal. The appellants appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the appeal could not be filed within the period of limitation prescribed by the Limitation Act, 1908, and that no appeal could be filed within that period. The High court held that the application for review was barred by limitation. The appellants contended that the Tribunal could not have entertained the appeal on the ground that the Tribunal did not have jurisdiction to pass the final order under section 23 of the Act as the Tribunal had not passed the final order. The High Courts, however, rejected the contention of the appellants that the Tribunal 's order was erroneous and the Tribunal was bound to pass an ex parte order under section 24 of the Act on the ground of limitation. The High courts, however, dismissed the appeal on merits. The appellants then appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The Tribunal was competent in the exercise of its powers under section 18 and the Tribunal had jurisdiction to pass such an order under sections 19 and 19 of that Act. The High Tribunal was not justified in holding that the Tribunal failed to pass an exparte order under section 25 of the Act in view of the provisions of section 18 of that Act and that it could not have passed an order under the provisions or section 19 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1901 and that the High Court was not justified to pass an erroneous order under section 21 of the Act because the Tribunal had failed to pass the ex parte order. [619 D] (2) The Tribunal had no power to pass an appellate order under section 22 of the Act to the Tribunal. The Tribunal was not entitled to review the order under the Act. [620 D] (3) The Tribunal could not pass an order on the application for revision under section 18 or section 19. [621 D] (4) The Tribunal did not pass an exparte order under section 27 of the Act unless the Tribunal had passed an order.

[602 B] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding the temple as a public temple, and that the appellant was not entitled under the Hindu law to the benefit conferred by the Hindu Succession. The respondent was the owner of the property in dispute. The respondent was the purchaser of the property. The tax cannot be levied on motor motor vehicles. It is a tax levied on the motor motor vehicles and motor motor vehicles, but the tax is levied on motor cars. The appellants, who were employed in the manufacture of sugar, were employed in a manufacturing unit in the manufacture and sale of sugar. The workmen were employed in manufacturing sugar. The appellants were employed in different industries in the manufacture. The workmen claimed that the workmen were entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Tribunal held that the workmen had been employed in different factories in the same industry and that the workmen should be treated as workmen. The Tribunal also held that the appellants were entitled to a benefit of the Act. The Tribunal, however, held that the employees were entitled to wages for the period of their employment. The Tribunal further held that the wages for the purpose of the Act were not the same as the wages for which the workmen were employed. The Tribunal accordingly held that the workers were entitled to equal wages for the purposes of the Act and that the wages of the workmen were not the basis for the Tribunal to determine the question of wages. The Tribunal however held that the Tribunal was right in holding that the workmen could be treated as employees of the manufacturing unit. The Tribunal therefore held that the employers were entitled to full wages for the entire period of their service. The Tribunal allowed the appeals and held that the wage of the workmen was not the same. The Tribunal in appeal held that the employer was entitled to the benefits of the Act, and that the Tribunal had not given any reasons for the Tribunal 's award. The Tribunal was also right in holding the workmen entitled to the same. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Tribunal erred in holding that there was no evidence to show that the workmen employed in the manufacturing unit were employed in any other industry. HELD: (i) The Tribunal was right when the workmen were working in the manufacturing units in the same trade. The Tribunal had not applied the principle of equal wages for equal work. The Tribunal has not given any reason for the Tribunal in fixing the wages of workmen. The workmen are entitled to the equal wages for each of them. [619 F G] (ii) The Tribunal has given reasons for the award of the Tribunal. The Tribunal is right in holding in the appeals to the Tribunal. [620 F] (iii) The Tribunal had given reasons for its award. The reasons given by the Tribunal in support of the award are not sufficient to justify the award. The award is set aside. The Tribunal will give reasons for its decision.

The appellant was a workman of the respondent company. The respondent was a workman in the respondent company and was a workman. The appellant was a member of the respondent. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and that he was not a person of the respondent and that the respondent had no right of continue in the appellant 's service, and that it was not a dispute between the parties. The appellant had no locus standi to continue in his service. The respondent had no locus to continue in that service. The order of the Industrial Tribunal was not a decree of a civil court. The appellant could not have been dismissed by the Industrial Tribunal. The order was not a final order. The appellant, therefore, was not entitled to continue in service. The appeal must be dismissed. The appellant 's appeal must be allowed. The order must be set aside. The appellant must be deemed to have been dismissed. The order should be set aside and the order should be restored.

The appellant, a company, was a registered company under the provisions of the , and the appellant was a registered society under the provisions and the appellant 's employer was a registered employer under the , and was a registered employee under the ,. The appellant was a 'registered employee ' under the , as defined in the Act. The appellant 's employers ' were not registered employees under the , but were registered employees under section 2(1) of the , as they were registered employees. The appellant contended that the appellant was not a 'registered employer ' under the . The appellant contended, that the appellant had been registered employees under sections 2(1), 2(1)(a) and 2(1). The appellant contended: (i) that the appellant ' was not a registered employee and was not a "registered employee" under the ,; (ii) that the provisions of section 2(2) of the Act were not applicable to the appellant '; (iii) that the Act was not applicable to a registered employee; and (iv) that the employees were not registered employers under the , because the appellant was registered employees under that Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i). The appellant was not registered employers and was not registered employees. It was not a mere registered employer under section 2 (1) of that Act. The Act was not a law for the time being in force. The Act did not apply to a registered employer. The Act could not be applied to a registered establishment under the , to which the Act was applicable. [615H; 715A] (ii) The Act was a law for a registered employer and was not applicable in the State of Gujarat. The Act had no application to a registered employers. The Act is a law for that purpose. The Act does not apply to the appellant. The Act has no application to the appellant because the Act is a statutory enactment. [616B] (iii) The Act is not a law in force in the State. The Act cannot be applied to the appellant as it is a law in the State and is not a statutory enactment, it is not open to the appellant to contend that the Act is not applicable to it. [617C] (iv) The Act does no help the appellant. [618E] (v) The Act has a statutory force and is not applicable in respect of the appellant '. [619A] (vi) The Act cannot apply to a new establishment. The Act can be applied to all the establishments. [620F] (vii) The Act can not be applied in respect of a registered employer, but it is a statutory provision. [621A] (viii) The Act must be construed in a manner which is not in the nature of a statutory provision and it cannot be applied in the present case. [622B] (ix) The Act, therefore, cannot be applied retrospectively to a registered registered employer. [623C] (x) The Act being a statutory provision, it cannot be said that the Act has no retrospective application to the establishment. [627F] (xi) The Act could be applied retrospectively in respect of an establishment.

The petitioners are engaged in the work of mining operations in the State of Madhya Pradesh. They were engaged in the mining operations in their respective areas. The High Courts have not committed any error in holding the petitioners to be entitled to the benefits of the Scheme and the High Courts have committed error in holding them to be entitled for the benefits of Scheme. [630B] 2. The High court has not committed any mistake in holding the petitioner to be entitled. The High courts have committed error of law in holding that there is no error of law. [631C] 3. The HighCourt has not committed error of fact in holding that in the absence of any material to show that the petitioners are entitled to the same benefits. [632C] 4. The plaintiffs were the owners of the land in dispute. The plaintiffs were the owner of the land. The plaintiffs claimed that the plaintiffs were entitled to the benefit of the lease. The plaintiffs contended that the plaintiffs had no right to the benefit under the lease. Held, that the plaintiffs could not be said to have acquired any right to the property in dispute. It was not necessary to prove that the plaintiffs acquired any right of the property in question. The plaintiffs had no title to the property. The plaintiffs could not prove that the defendants acquired any right or title to the properties. The plaintiffs did not prove that they acquired any right in the property. It was only when the plaintiffs acquired the right of the plaintiffs to the property, that the defendants were entitled to a decree for possession. The plaintiffs failed to prove that they were entitled to any relief. The plaintiffs was entitled to the relief. The defendants were entitled only to the relief of possession. The defendants could not prove the right of possession. Held, further, that the suit was not barred by section 14 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. The plaintiffs ' right to the relief was not barred under section 14 of Limitation Act. The plaintiffs must prove that they had acquired any right which was acquired by them. The plaintiffs cannot prove that they did not acquire any right of title to the land. It was also not necessary to establish that the plaintiffs did not acquire the right of ownership. The plaintiffs should prove that they possessed any right of ownership in the property in suit. The plaintiffs would prove that they purchased the property in the suit. The defendants did not prove the title of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs, therefore, could not prove their right of ownership on the basis of the sale deed. The plaintiffs also failed to prove the title. The plaintiffs therefore, could prove that they obtained the right of title.

The High Courts were right in holding the appellant guilty of the charge. [630 H] (ii) The High court was right in reversing the order of acquittal. [631 H] (iii) The High Courts had not committed any error in holding that there was no evidence of the prosecution to prove the charge. The High courts were right in reversing that order. [632 H] (iv) The High courts had not committed an error in holding the accused guilty of the offence. [633 H] (v) The HighCourt was right in interfering with the order of the High Court. [634 A] (vi) The High Judge was right in taking the view that the evidence was not reliable. [635 H] (vii) The High judge was right in coming to the conclusion that the evidence had not been reliable and the High Court was in error in holding so. The appellant was a public limited company carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling of water in the city of Bombay. The appellant was a local authority. The appellant applied for permission to establish a factory for the purpose of carrying on the said business. The appellant made a complaint to the District Magistrate, Bombay, alleging that the appellant had committed a breach of the provisions of the Bombay Municipal Act, 1922, and that the appellant was not entitled to the permission under section 7(1) of the Act. The District Magistrate, after considering the report of the District Magistrate and the report of a District Magistrate, held that the appellant 's application for permission was not maintainable. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the District Magistrate was not competent to grant the permission under article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution. The High court held that the permission was not necessary and that the District Collector was competent to grant it. The appellant contended that the District Judge was not competent in the matter of granting the permission under the Act. Held, that the District Court was not competent under article 133 (1)(a), and that the permission under that article was not necessary. The District Judge was right in holding that the permission granted under section 7 (1) of Act was not necessary, and that it was necessary to grant the consent under section 7 of the Act, and that, therefore, the District Magistrate could not grant the permission. The District Court was right in rejecting the contention of the appellant that the permission of the District Collector under section 7 was not necessary because the District Magistrate had no jurisdiction to grant the sanction under section 7. The District judge was right in dismissing the petition. The High Courts were right in holding the appellant 'to have the permission under sub section (1) (a) of section 7.

The respondent was a railway servant in the railway station. The railway was charged with theft of railway goods. The railway authorities found that the railway was not a railway servant. The railway administration charged with theft. The railway authority convicted the railway servant under section 3(1) (a) (i) (i). The railway authorities convicted the railway servants under section 3 (1) (i), (ii) and (iii) of the Act. The High Court, on appeal, held that the railway administration charged the railway servant guilty of the offence under section 3 of the Act and sentenced him to imprisonment for a term of three years. The High court, on appeal by special leave, held that section 3(2) (i)(a) (ii) of the . Held, that the railway authorities were not entitled to the benefit of section 3(3) (i); that the railway servant was not a Railway servant and was not a person in possession of goods. The Railway administration charged with the theft of railway property. The railway servant was therefore not entitled to any benefit of section 4(1) of the. Act. The railway court was right in holding that the railway had no authority to deal with the goods. The High Courts were right in holding the railway servant liable to be convicted under section 3. The railway Administration was not entitled to benefit of section 5(1) because the railway administration had no authority under section 3 to deal with goods. The fact that the railway authority had no authority in law to deal with them was not sufficient to hold that the railway property was a railway property.

The respondent landlord, a tenant of a shop, was the tenant of the respondent landlord. The respondent landlord, in the suit, filed a suit for eviction of the appellants on the ground that the appellants had not been in possession of the premises in question. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellants filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that the appellants were in possession of a shop in the premises in dispute and that the respondent landlord was not in possession of any premises in dispute. The High court held that the respondent tenant was in possession of that premises in dispute, and that the appellants was in possession thereof. The High Courts, however, held that the appellant was in possession and that the appellant had not been able to establish that the respondent was in possession or that he was in possession. The High. Court held that since the respondent landlord had not been a tenant of the premises, the appellants were not entitled to the protection of section 14(1)(e) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1956. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the appellants 's tenancy was not a tenancy of the premises. The appellants were in occupation of the premises and were in possession thereof, and therefore, the respondent was not entitled to protection of section 15(1)(d) of the Act. [797E] 2.2 The High Court has not considered the question whether the appellants were tenants of the premises or not. The High 's finding that the appellants are tenants of the respondent, was not correct. The HighCourt was right in coming to the conclusion that the appellants have not been in occupation of any premises. [798E] 2:3 The High Court, therefore, was right in taking the view that the appellants could not be in possession of premises in dispute as they were in possession and were in occupation thereof. [799E] 2 :4 The High Court erred in holding that since the appellants were the tenants of the shop in dispute, they were not entitled for protection of section 13(1)(c) of the Rent and Eviction Act. [899E] 3:4 The High Courts have not considered the relevant provisions of the Act and the High Court has rightly held that the tenants were in occupation and were in the occupation of the same. [702E] 2.:5 The High Court had not considered the provisions of the Rent Act and the Rent Act. [602E] 3.1 The appellants were tenants in the premises and they were in occupation. They were in occupation, and were in their occupation. They had not been evicted from the premises. They were not in occupation of that premises. They had been in occupation. Their occupation was not in occupation. The appellants had not taken any steps to evict them from the premises in their occupation, and they were not in possession thereof and they were entitled to protection under section 14(2)(e). [703E] 3 :4 The appellants were not in actual occupation of the shop. They were therefore entitled to protection. [704E] 3.:5 The appellants were inducted as tenants of the appellant. They were tenants of a shop. They had also not been in the occupation. They could not be evicted from the said premises. They could be evicted from that premises. [603E] 2.(6) The High Court rightly held that since they were in the possession of the respondent they were in their possession and were not in the occupation thereof. They were also in occupation of their premises. They cannot be evicted from their premises.

The appellant, a company, was a company incorporated under the Bihar Electricity Supply Act, 1948. The appellant was a company carrying on business in the State of Bihar. The appellant, a Company, was a public limited company. The company was a public company. The appellant had been carrying on business of the company. The State Government, however, issued a notification under section 3 of the Act on the basis of which the company was carrying on business. The appellant contended that the company was not a public limited Company and that the company had no power to carry on business in that State. The State of Bihar, however, contended that the Company was not a private limited company and that the Company had no power or authority to carry on its business in that state. The State, however, urged that the Company could not be said to be a public limited undertaking. The Tribunal, however, held that the Company did not carry on its own business in the state. The Tribunal held that the company could not carry on business of its own. The Tribunal also held that the Board had no power and authority to carry out its business in the manner prescribed by the Act. The Tribunal accordingly held that the appellant was not a 'public limited company ' and that the Board was not a "public limited company" within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Act. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the Tribunal was right in holding that the Company 's business was not a commercial undertaking within the meaning Of section 2(2)(d) and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to carry on the business in the sense of section 2 (1)(d). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal was right when the Company was carrying on its own, it was not open to the State Government to carry on any business in the same State. The Tribunal had no power under section 2(3)(d) to carry on it. [601 B] 2. The Tribunal has not given any reasons for the Tribunal to come to the conclusion that the Company has not been carrying on its business. The Tribunal is therefore right in holding the Company ' to carry on their own business in that area. [602 B] 3. The Tribunal cannot be said to have acted in a manner which is not permissible under section 2 (2)(d). [602 C] 4. The Tribunal could not have taken into account the fact that the Company is carrying on its trading in the State.

The respondent was married to one Shri Rambhai, the appellant and his wife. The respondent was married on January 1, 1973. The High Courts were right in holding the respondent ' guilty of cruelty under section 125 (1)(d). [703F] 3. The High 's order was not based on any evidence. P.C. and the High Court was in error in holding that it was not a case where the respondent was a 'wife " within the meaning or clause (d). [807E] 7. The High. Court was right. The appellant was the owner of the land in dispute. The respondents were the owners of the land. The respondents filed a suit for possession of the land on the ground that the land was not a private land. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the land in question was a private land and that the land had been acquired by the State Government under the provisions of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879. The High court held that the lands were not private land and the land was acquired by the Government under the Land Revenue Code. The High Courts held that the suit was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the land acquired by the appellant was private land and was not private land. [630E] The High Court had not considered the evidence on record and the High Court was in error in holding that it was not a public land. [730E] In the instant case, the land was private land. It was not a land. The land was acquired for the purpose of the State Government. The land in question had been acquired for the purposes of the State. The land had been taken over by the State. It was therefore not a private property. The land could not be acquired for the benefit of the State, and the land could not have been acquired for any other purpose. [731E] The land was not private property. It was a private property and was not a property. The State Government had no authority to acquire the land for the purposes for which it was acquired. The land acquired by it was not private lands. The land did not belong to the State. [732E] The State Government was not competent to acquire the lands for the purposes mentioned in the Schedule to the Act. The land, therefore, could not be said to be private property.

The appellant was charged with the offence of criminal conspiracy under section 120B of the Indian Penal Code, and was charged with an offence under section 120 B of the Indian Evidence Act, and was convicted under section 120A of the Indian Indian Penal Code. The High Court held that the appellant was guilty of criminal conspiracy and convicted him under section 120(b) of the Indian IPC. The High court held that the offence of conspiracy was not proved. Held, that the appellant had been guilty of criminal misconduct and was not guilty of criminal breach of trust. The appellant was not guilty under section 120 of the Indian Code. The appellant had been convicted under section 5(1)(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The appellant could not be convicted under section 4(1)(b) of that Act. The appellant did not fall within the definition of "public servant" in section 2(1)(c) of the Act. The High Courts were right in holding that the appellant could not have been convicted under the Indian Penal code. The appellant 's conviction under section 120 A of the Indian penal Code was not based on any evidence. The appellant, therefore, was not entitled to be convicted under the Act. Held, further, that the offence under section 5 (1)(a)(a) was not proved and the appellant was not entitled under section 5 of the Indian Criminal Procedure Code. The question whether the appellant was a public servant was not decided by the High Court. Held, also, that the expression "public servant " in section 2 (1)(c)()()()(a) means a public servant " in the sense of a public servant. The expression "public servants" in section 5(2)(a) is not defined in the Act. It is not necessary that the expression must be understood in the context of the expression "Public servant" in the context in which it occurs. The expression 'public servant" is not defined. The expression must be construed in the context. The expression used in section 2 of the Indian Police Act is not defined as a "public servant". The expression "Public Servant" in section 3(1)(d) means a person who is employed in connection with the affairs of the State or of any State or of a State. The expression in section 2 means a person employed in connection therewith or in connection with any affairs of the Union or of a Union or of any of the States or of any other State or of the State. The word "public servant", in section 2, means a person in connection with or in connection therewith. The expression is not defined by the Act.

The Respondent No. 1, a tenant of the Respondent No. 2, was the owner of the property in dispute. The Respondent No. 3, a tenant, was the proprietor of the property. [636D] 2. The Respondent had no title to the property in question. The Respondent could not be said to be the owner of any property in dispute, and that the respondent was the owner. [637D] 3. [638D] 4. The Trial court was right in holding that the Respondent could not have any title to it. [639D] 5. The Respondent did not prove that the property in suit was the ownership of Respondent No.3. [640D] 6. The Respondent having failed to prove the title of the Respondent, she could not be held to be the owners of any property.

The appellant was the owner of a land in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The land was acquired by the Government under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The notification under section 3(1) was not applicable in the case in which the land was acquired. The notification was not applicable because the land was not acquired. The Collector had no power to issue the notification under the Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1961. [630E] 2. The notification issued under section 6 was not applicable. The notification had not been issued under section 4. The notification could not be issued under section 3. The notification did not apply to the case where the land was purchased. The notification in question was issued under section 5. The Collector was not competent to issue the said notification under section 5, but the Collector had jurisdiction to issue such a notice. [731E] 4. The Collector could not have issued the notice under the Land Reform Act, 1961 to the appellant. [732E] 5. The Collector has no jurisdiction to pass the order under section 6, but he had no jurisdiction in the matter. The Collector cannot issue the notice in question.

The appellant was elected as a member of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960. The appellant could not be said to have been elected as member of the Society. The appellant 's election was not challenged by the appellant. The appellant did not file any appeal against that order. [501B C] 2.2 The appellant was not elected as a Chairman of the Maharashtra Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act. The order of the Registrar was not challenged in the High Court and the appellant was entitled to be elected as a President of the Maharashtra Society. [502C] 3.3 The appellant was a member of Maharashtra State Cooperative Bank. He was elected as member. He was not elected. He was disqualified under the provisions of the Maharashtra Act. [503C] 4.4 The appellant was duly elected as a result of the election. He was declared elected as a Director of the Maharashtra Government. He was also elected as a Managing Director. He was duly elected. He had been elected as the Managing Director. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the election of his Chairman. The High court dismissed the writ petitions. [505C] 5.4 The High Court was right in holding that the appellant could not have been elected. He was entitled to continue as a member. He could not be elected as the member. He had not filed an appeal against the election of a member. The appellant has not filed any writ petition challenging the election. [507C] 5:6. The appellant is a member of an Maharashtra State Cooperative Cooperative Society. He was a member. His election was challenged by the respondent. He was dismissed by the Maharashtra Cooperative Society. He has filed an appeal before the Maharashtra State Government. He has not filed an application for setting aside the election. The appellant also filed an appeal. The Maharashtra State Cooperative Society has filed an application before the Maharashtra Cooper Societies Act. He has also filed an application under Section 29 of the Maharashtra Societies Act. [603D] 6.6. The Maharashtra Co operative Society is a society registered under the Maharashtra Coorg Societies Act. It is a society which is registered under the Act. It has been registered under the provisions and the society has been registered. The appellant, therefore, cannot be said that he was elected as the Chairman of the Society under the Maharashtra Act and the appellant has not been elected. [508C] 7.7. The appellant having filed an appeal to this court, the appellant cannot be held to be a person elected as a director. [509F] 7.8. The appellant being a member of that Maharashtra State Cooperative Union, is not entitled to be declared elected as the members of the Maharashtra Legislative Assembly.

The appellants were the tenants of the premises in dispute. They were the tenants in respect of the premises. The appellants filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the appellants had not been given a licence under section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary Powers) Act, 1947, and that the appellants were not entitled to the protection of section 3(2) of the Act. The appellants contended that the appellants ' claim was barred by section 3(3) of the . Held, that the appellants could not be granted a licence under the Act. Section 3(1)(a) of the , does not apply to a suit for ejectment on the ground of bona fide requirement of the landlord. The appellants were not the tenants of a premises in dispute and they were not entitled under section 3 (1) of that Act. The provisions of section 3 (2) of that section are not applicable to a suit under the Act, and the appellants were entitled to the benefit of section 3 of the Act, because they were not the landlords of the premises, and the provisions of section 4(1) are not applicable in the case of a suit under section 3 of that Act, and that they were not liable to be evicted on the ground, that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the suit under section 4(2) and that the provisions contained in section 3(4) of the. Act were not attracted. The appellants had not given a licence to the appellants under section 3. The appellants could not therefore be granted a certificate under section 3, because they had not given the licence to the respondents under section 3 and that they had not been granted a licence. The appellants did not give a licence to them under section 3 as they were not in possession of the premises and were not entitled for the protection of the Act on the ground which they had not applied. The appellants therefore could not be said to have been granted a certificate. The appellants ' claim to be barred by section 4(3) was not barred by section 5(1) and the appellants could be said to be not entitled to a decree under section 3 or section 3 of this Act.

The appellant, a member of the Indian Administrative Service, was appointed as a member of a Public Service Commission. The respondent was a tenant of the land in dispute. The respondent was a cultivating tenant of the lands in dispute. He was a tenant in the land. [741C] (5) The High 'Court was in error not in holding that section 2(2) of the Act was applicable to the land in respect of which the land belonged. [742C] (6) The HighCourt was in wrong error in holding the land as such. [744C] (7) The High Power was not justified in holding that it was not a cultivating tenancy but a cultivating tenant 's holding was a cultivating tenants. [743C] (8) The High power was not justified. [745C] (9) The High Judge was in error error in holding in holding that since the land in a cultivating tenancy is a cultivating tenant it was not open to the High Court to hold that the land is a cultivating tenancy as such. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the plaintiffs could claim the compensation in respect of the estate which was held by the deceased to be the heirs of the deceased in the estate of a deceased person. The High Courts were right in holding the suit to be maintainable. [630 F] (ii) The High court was right in dismissing the suit. The High 's decision was erroneous. The HighCourt was right in rejecting the suit. [631 F] (iii) The High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. It was not open to the High Court to interfere with the decision of the High Court. [632 F] (iv) The HighCourt had no jurisdiction in the matter of the claim of the plaintiffs. The High. Court was right when it held that the claim of compensation for their estate was not maintainable, and the High Court was in error in holding that it was not open for the High Court in holding that there was no right to sue for the compensation for death of the plaintiffs, and that the claim was not maintainable in view of the provisions of section 5 of the Limitation Act. [633 F] (v) The High Power under section 5 of Limitation Act was not a statutory power and the High court was in error. [634 F] (vi) The High.Court was in error when it held the suit to have been barred by the Limitation Act, and the suit was barred by the principles of res judicata. [635 F] (vii) The High 'Court was in wrong in holding that in the present case the claim for damages for the death was not maintainable and the High Courts were in error in dismissing the appeal. [636 F] (viii) The High power under section 5 was not a judicial power and the power of the High court to entertain the claim for payment of compensation for death was not a matter of discretion. [637 F G] (ix) The Highness of the High Power was in error and was not justified. [638 F] (x) The High courts were right in rejecting it. [639 F] (xi) The High jurisdiction of the High Courts under section 5 is not a statutory one. [640 F] (xii) The High Level was not justified because the claim of damages for the estate for the death or death of the heirs of a deceased in the case of a deceased, was not maintainable under section 5. [641 F] (xiii) The High-Court was in right in holding in favour of the plaintiffs and the High Power under the Limitation Act was in error error in holding the claim for a claim for the death.

The appellants were the tenants of the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for eviction of the appellants on the ground that the appellants were not the tenants of a building. [693 G] The appellant was not a landlord of the premises and the appellants had no right to the benefit.

The appellants were convicted under section 3(1) of the Punjab Security of Supplies Act, 1951, and sentenced to imprisonment for a term of five years. They were guilty of an offence under section 4(1) (a) of the Act and they were not guilty of the offences under the Act, and they were liable to be convicted under section 5(1) read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. The appellant was a workman of the Madras State. The workmen were paid wages for the period of their service. The workmen challenged the validity of the order of the Tribunal on the ground that the workmen were not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Madras Labour Act, 1948. The Tribunal held that the workmen had been guilty of misconduct and that the workmen could not be dismissed from service. The Tribunal also held that the workers were not entitled for the benefit of section 25(1) of the Act. The Tribunal, however, held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 25(2) of the Madras Act. The appellant appealed to the Tribunal. The Tribunal set aside the order of dismissal and directed the appellant to pay the wages for the periods of their service and to pay the same to the workmen. The Tribunal further held that the workman was not entitled for any relief under the Act. Held, that the workmen was not entitled under section 25 (1) of that Act to be dismissed from services. The Tribunal was right in holding that the workmen did not fall within the definition of "workman" in section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The workmen had not been dismissed from service because they were not entitled under the Act to the benefit under section 25. The Tribunal had not given any finding on the question whether the workmen were entitled to the benefits under section 25 of the Act or not. The Tribunal therefore held that the appellants were not entitled either to the benefit or the benefit of sections 25 and 26 of the Act and that the Tribunal was right to hold that the workmen fell within the definition. The Tribunal accordingly held that the question whether they were entitled to any benefit under section 26 of the Industrial Dispute Act was not a question of law.

The appellant filed an application under Rule 15 of the Punjab Election Rules, 1951 for setting aside the election of the respondent. The High Court dismissed the application. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the election of respondent was not maintainable because the election petition had been dismissed by the trial Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was in error by holding that the petition was not barred by limitation. The High Courts were in error in rejecting the application. [601C] 2. The High Judge was in error of holding that the application was not maintainable and the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the application. The High 's order was set aside by the High court. [602C] 3. The High Powered Court is not competent to entertain the petition. The High power of the High Court is not a Court of appeal. The High is not competent in the exercise of its power under Rule 15. [603D] 4. The High Procedure Code is a special provision and it is not a special provision. The High. Court is not empowered to entertain the election petition. The power of the Court is not to be exercised in a routine manner. [604D] 5. The HighCourt is not competent under the Code to entertain the appeal. The power to entertain the suit is not to have the power to entertain it. [605D] 6. The High courts are not competent to exercise its power under rule 15. [703D] 7. The High High Court is in error in dismissing the petition.

The appellant was appointed as a teacher in the State of Uttar Pradesh. He was appointed as an Assistant teacher in the Government Higher Secondary School. He was confirmed in the post of Assistant teacher. He was promoted as a teacher on the basis of a selection list. He was also appointed as a Principal in the Government Secondary School. The appellant was appointed on the basis that he was appointed as Principal in the State. He was further appointed as a Head teacher in the said school. He was given a charge of a teacher in a school. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appointment of the appellant was illegal and void. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment of the teacher in the school was illegal and invalid. The appointment was illegal and the appointment was illegal. [615H; 715A] 2. The appointment is illegal and void and the appointment is illegal. [715F] 3. The appointment has been made by the appellant on the basis thereof. The appointment cannot be made by the management. The appointment can be made by a person who is appointed as a Headmaster in the Government Primary School. The appointment must be made by an authority competent to do so. [716A] 4. The appointment made by the Management is illegal and invalid and the appointment cannot be said to be illegal. [816F] 5. The appointment in question is illegal and the appellant is not entitled to any relief. [717F] 6. The appointment to the post of Principal in the school is illegal. The appointment itself is illegal and is void. [718F] 7. The appointment by the management is illegal and illegal. [917F] 8. The appointment order is illegal and it is not open to the appellant to challenge the appointment of a teacher on a selection list on the ground that the appointment was not illegal. [1017F] 9. The appointment under the Act is illegal and not void. [918F] 918A] 9. It is not open for the appellant to raise the contention that the appointment made by him was illegal and is not illegal. The appellant has not challenged the appointment of an Assistant teacher on the ground of the existence of a vacancy in the Government Middle School.

The petitioners were manufacturers of cotton yarn. They were also manufacturing cotton yarn. The petitioners were assessed to sales tax under the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1957. The petitioners challenged the validity of the assessment on the ground that the goods were not 'goods ' within the meaning of section 2(f) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the goods in question were 'goods ' and were not ' goods ' within the definition of 'goods '. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was in error in holding that the goods manufactured by the petitioners were 'goods within the meaning Of section 2(g) of the Rajasthan Sales tax Act, 1957 and were 'goods " within the meaningof section 2(h) of the said Act. [601D] The High Court has not properly appreciated the evidence on record and has come to the conclusion that the goods are 'goods ' in the sense of section 2 (g) of that Act. [701D] In the instant case, the petitioners were manufacturing cotton yarn and were not "goods" within the meaning given to section 2(j) of the Sales Tax Act. [801D] It is well settled that the goods must be 'goods ' under the Act. [901D] Commissioner of Sales Tax, Rajasthan vs M/s. M.K. Jain & Co., ; , referred to. The High court was in error by holding that the petitioners were "goods" under the Act and were not entitled to the benefit of the said provisions.

The respondent company was a company carrying on business in the manufacture of coal and coal. The respondent company was carrying on the business of coal and cement. The respondent was employed as a worker in the factory. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of transfer. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a writ application in the High court challenging the validity and validity of the transfer order. The High court dismissed the writ application. The appellant contended that the transfer order was vitiated by mala fides and that the transfer was vitiated by malafide and that the order was vitiated because it was not passed in accordance with law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The transfer order is vitiated by mala fide and is vitiated by malafide. [601D] 2. The transfer is vitiated by malafides. The transfer of the respondent is vitiated by non fides. [602D] 3. The transfer cannot be said to be vitiated by mala mala fides. [702D] 4. The transfer can be said to have been made in accordance with the rules of natural justice. [703D] 5. The transfer has to be made in accordance to the rules of the natural justice. The transfer must be made in conformity with the rules. [704D] 6. The transfer may be made in compliance with the rules and the rules of procedure. [705D] 7. The transfer does not amount to mala fide. [707D] 7: The transfer is not a matter of policy. [706D] 8. The transfer, therefore, is not vitiated by mala malafide. [709D] 9. The transfer was made in accordance accordance with the provisions of the Act. [710F] 9. In the instant case, the transfer was made by the respondent in accordance with rules of procedure and the rules. The transfer made in accordance therewith was not in accordance with any rules of procedure or rules. [606D] 9: The transfer was not in compliance with any rules.

The respondent, a company, was a registered company carrying on business in the appellant 's business in the respondent 's business. The respondent, a registered company, was carrying on business as a registered company. The respondent was a registered trade union. The respondent applied for permission to the appellant to establish a trade union. In the application for permission to establish a Trade union, the appellant contended that the application was not maintainable as the application was made in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. The appellant contended that it was not a trade union within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Act. Held, that the application for leave to establish a new trade union was not maintainable. The application was not a reference to the Industrial Tribunal. The application for permission was not maintainable because the application was in accordance with section 2(2) of the . The application was made by the appellant in accordance with law. The application made by the respondent was not a 'appeal ' within the meaning Of section 2(3) of the , and the application was therefore not maintainable. Held, further, that the reference was not a dispute within the meaningof section 2(4) of the and the application for the permission was not a question of law. The reference was not an appeal within the meaning ofs. 2(3). The application was therefore maintainable. The reference must be made in accordance to the provisions of section 2 (3) of that Act. The application must be made within the meaning and of section 2. The application is not a reference within the meaning given to the Act. The reference is not a dispute of fact. The reference cannot be made in a proceeding under the Act.

The appellant imported a motor vehicle for the purpose of carrying passengers in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The Notification No. 7/75 dated 29.03. 75 was applicable to the goods covered by the said Notification No.8/75 dated 26.03. 76. [703E] 2. The Notification was not a notification issued under the said Notification. The Notification itself was not applicable. The Notification also did not apply to the goods which were covered by the earlier Notification No. 11/75 dated 24.03. 77. [704E] 3. The Notification dated 28.3.75 was applicable to motor vehicles. The Notification did not apply in the case. The Notification does not apply to motor vehicles covered by the latter Notification. [705E] 4. The Notification is not applicable to motor vehicle. The Notification cannot be applied to motor vehicles, as the Notification itself was applicable to a motor vehicle. [707E] 5. The Notification in question is not applicable in respect of motor vehicles.

In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit was not maintainable as the plaintiffs had not been able to establish the right of the plaintiffs to the suit properties and that the suit properties were not ancestral properties and that they were not ancestral property. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The plaintiffs had not established the right of pre pority to the suit property. The plaintiffs were not entitled to the relief of pre pourity. The plaintiffs have not established the existence of any right of pre nority to a suit properties. They have not established any right of the defendants to the suit. The plaintiffs are entitled to the reliefs of pre pureity. [601B] 2. The plaintiffs ' right of pre mority to an institution is not a right of pre tority. The right of pre emption to an institution cannot be denied merely because the right of preemption is not a part of the right of a pre emption. [602B] 3. The right to pre emption is a right of preemption. The right is a right to pre morority. It is a right which is a right in the pre emption and the right of re emption is not a matter of right. The right cannot be denied unless it is established that the right of self emption is an absolute right. [603B] 4. The right in the institution is a right and the right to pre porities is a right. The rights of pre emptority cannot be denied if it is established by the parties that the right is an absolute one. [604C] 5. The right which is an absolute and absolute right is a part of right and the rights of pre morsity are not absolute. [605C] 6. The right conferred by the right to preemption is a right, which is a part and parcel of right. [703F] 7. The right under the right to property is a right conferred by a right of re quest is a right on the person who has right to pre pre emption, and the right is a matter of law. [606F] 7: The right of preemption cannot be denied because the right to re emption was a right of the pre emptors to the institution. [607F] 8. The right claimed by pre emption cannot be denied when the right of cross emption is claimed by pre morities. [608F] 9. The right given to pre emptee to an institution can be denied if the right is claimed by the pre em emption. The right can be denied only if the right of inter emption is denied. [609F] 9: The right to preemption can be denied when there is a right claimed by the parties.

The appellant was a railway employee in the Railway. He was paid a monthly salary of Rs. 100/ per month. He was entitled to the salary of Rs . . . . The respondent was paid a salary of Rs.. . . . He was paid monthly salary of the appellant. The respondent was not paid any monthly salary of his service. The respondent 's claim was that he was entitled to a salary of the respondent. Held, that the appellant had been paid monthly salary for the period of his service and the respondent was entitled to payment of monthly salary of that period. The respondent had not been paid any monthly monthly salary of her service. The appellant was entitled under the provisions of the Railway Establishment Act, 1948. The respondent could not be said to be a railway employee. The respondent did not fall within the definition of " railway employee" in section 2(h) of the Act.
