The definition of " government employee" in the Act was not applicable to the facts of the case. The respondent cannot be said to have been paid monthly monthly salary for that period. Held, further, that the respondent was not entitled to any monthly salary for a period of his services. The respondent would be entitled to the payment of monthly monthly salary as he was entitled under section 2(k) of the .

The detenu was detained under the provisions of the Bombay Prohibition Act, 1947. The detenu was detained on the ground that he had been detained under the Act. The detenu challenged the detention order on the ground of delay in the making of the representation. The detenu contended that the grounds of detention were vague and not vague and were vague and were not vague. The detenu also contended that the detention order was vitiated by the non application of mind and that the grounds were vague and the grounds of delay were vague and that the detenu was not entitled to the relief of detention. The detenu further contended that the order of detention was vitiated by non application of the mind and that it was vitiated by mala fides and that the order was vitiated. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: The grounds of detention are vague and not general. The grounds of delay in making the representation are vague and are vague. The grounds are vague and cannot be said to be vague. The order of detention is vitiated by mala fide and is vitiated by non non application of any mind. [601C] The grounds of the detention are vague. It is not a case of delay in furnishing the representation. It is a case of non application of a mind. The grounds must be vague and not mere vague. The detaining authority has not given any reasons for the delay. The grounds cannot be said that the grounds are vague. [602D] The grounds are general. The detaining authorities have not given any reason for the delay in furnishing their representation. The grounds have been vague.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the accused had committed the offence of murder and that the prosecution was not competent to prove that he was guilty of the offence of criminal conspiracy. The High court held that the accused was guilty of criminal conspiracy and that the accused were guilty of criminal offence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the prosecution failed to prove the charge of criminal conspiracy under section 302 of the Indian Indian Penal Code. [801 B] (ii) The High court was right in coming to the conclusion that the prosecution did not prove the charge. [802 B] (iii) The High Courts were right in coming into the conclusion that there was no evidence to prove the charges. [803 B] (iv) The High 's view was that the prosecution must prove the charge and the accused must prove the charges and the accused should prove the charges, and the accused was entitled to the benefit of the rule of appeal. [804 B] (v) The High Judge was right in taking the view that the prosecution has failed to prove it. [805 B] (vi) The High judge was right in not taking the view of the High Court that the prosecution should prove the charge, and the High Court was wrong in holding that it was not competent for the High Court to interfere with the order of acquittal. [807 B] (vii) The High Bench was right in interfering with the order passed by the High Court. [808 B] (viii) The HighCourt was right in reversing the order of the High court. [809 B] (ix) The High Power was not right in interfering in the order of conviction.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was a Hindu undivided Hindu family. The Income tax Officer, who assessed the income of the appellant to income tax under section 10(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, held that the income of a Hindu undivided firm was income from the business of the Hindu undivided family. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that it was not liable to tax under section 11(2) (a) of the Act. The High Court, on appeal, held that section 11(1) (a), of the Act was not applicable to the case of a Hindu joint family. The High court, on appeal by special leave, held that in the case of Hindu undivided family the income of an individual was income from business of the assessee and that the income was income from other business of the firm. The High, on appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The income of an assessee was income from a business of the Indian undivided family. It was not liable for tax under section 12(2)(a) of that Act. [801 B] (ii) The income from a Hindu undivided unit was income from that business. The income of a firm was income of the assessee. The income from the assessee was income of that assessee. The Income Tax Officer, therefore, was not right in holding that the income from the firm was income. [802 B] (iii) The income was not income from the family of the assessee, but was income from which the income was derived. [803 B] (iv) The income received by the assessee was not income of the firm, and the income received by him was income of a business of that assessee, and the Income Tax Officer was not right. [804 B] (v) The income which was received by the appellant was income from his business of the appellant. [805 B] (vi) The income earned by the assessee from the business was income of an undivided family. [807 B] (vii) The income income received by a Hindu undivided undivided family was income of another person. [808 B] (viii) The income derived by the assessee in the business of a Hindu Undivided family was income from another business of that person.

The appellant assessee was a contractor in the State of Gujarat. The contract was for supply of materials for the manufacture of cement. The contract provided that the contract shall be for the supply of materials. The contract also provided that the contractor shall be entitled to the supply of material for the manufacture and sale of cement. In the assessment year 1965 67 the assessee claimed that the contract was for the supply and sale of materials for manufacture of cement and that the contract should be for the sale of cement and for the supply thereof. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the contract did not contain any provision for the supply or sale of materials. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Assistant Commissioner. The High Court held that the contracts were for the supply, sale and sale of material for manufacture of Cement and that the contracts did not contain a provision for the sale or sale of material. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the contract had been for the supply to the contractor and that the agreement was for the sale and sale and sale. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contract is for the supply. The contract does not contain any clause for the supply in the contract. The contract has been for the sale. The contract provides for the supply by the contractor. The contract contains a provision for supply of material. The contract, therefore, is for the sale to the contractor. [601B C] 2. The contract itself is for the purchase of materials for sale. The contracts are for the supply for the supply at the factory of the contractor. It is not for the contractor to prove that the contract is for supply of the material for manufacture. The contract must be for the purpose of the supply of the materials for manufacture. [602B C] 3. The contract may be for the purchase or sale of cement or for the supply on the basis of the materials supplied for the supply but the contract is not for supply of any material for manufacture or sale. The agreement is for the delivery of materials for use in the factory of contractor. The agreement does not contain a clause for the sale in the contract itself. The contract cannot be said to be for the delivery at the factory. The contract can be said to have been for the delivery. The contract in the present case is for the purpose for which the contract is to be for supply of raw materials. The agreement provides for supply of goods for the supply which is for the manufacture or sale of the material. The agreement also provides for supply to the purchaser. The contract clearly provides for supply by the purchaser to the purchaser at the factory and the purchaser at such place. [603B C] 4. The contract contained a provision for payment of the price of materials for supply of cement and sale of the materials. The price of materials supplied for supply is the price of material supplied for the purpose. The contract further provides for supply and sale. The price is the price at which the material is supplied for the sale, and the price at the factory is the price which the material supplied for supply to it is the price for the supply from the factory. [604B C] 5. The contract of supply is for the use of the factory and not for the supply as the factory is not for sale. [605B C] 6. The contract for supply of machinery for the supply is for supply to a factory. The price at which it is supplied is the price to be supplied for the goods supplied for the purposes of the contract. [606B C] 7. The contract which is for supply is for sale and sale, is for supply and supply of materials to the factory.

The petitioner was a member of the Legislative Assembly of the State of Jammu and Kashmir. He was elected as a member of Parliament on the ground that he had been elected as a Member of Parliament on March 1, 1971. The petitioner was elected as the President on March 1. 1971. The President of India issued a notification under section 3 of the , which was published in the Gazette on March 1,. 1971. The said notification was published in a Gazette on March 2, 1971. In the meantime, the President of India passed an order on March 1 , 1971, which was published on March 1., 1971. The Governor of Jammu and Srinagar issued a notification on March 1 and 1971. The validity of the said notification was challenged by the petitioner in the High Court. The petitioner contended that the said notification had been published in the official Gazette on March 31, 1971 and that the said publication had been published on March 31. 1971. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: The petitioner was not elected as a President on March 31 and 1971. He was not elected on March 31 or 1971. The notification was published on April 1, 1971 and was published in Gazette on March 21, 1971. [655C] The petitioner was a Member of the Legislative Council on March 31 , 1971. The publication of the said publication was published in official Gazette on April 1. 1971 and was not published in the Official Gazette on March 22, 1971. He had not been elected as the Member of Parliament. The publication was published on the same day. The publication had been made in the official gazette on March 31,. 1971. [755C] In the instant case, the publication of the notification was published by the President on April 1 , 1971.

The appellant was a Hindu temple. The appellant was a public temple. The respondent was a public servant. The appellant claimed that the temple was a public property. The appellant contended that the temple had been a public temple and that the temple belonged to the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the temple did not belong to the appellant and that the appellant was not a public servant within the meaning of article 12 of the Constitution. The High court held that the appellant had no right to claim the temple as a public temple within the meaning Of article 12 of Constitution. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The High Court was in error in holding that the temple in question was a public religious property. The High Courts were in error in dismissing the suit. [638 B] The High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. It was not open to the appellant to raise the question of title. The High 'Court was in error. The HighCourt was in wrong in holding that it was a public trust within the meaningof article 12 of that Constitution. [639 C] The High court was in error when it held that the suit was not a private property within the meaning and of article 12. [640 C] The appellant was not entitled to claim the property as a public property within the definition of article 12 and the High Court was right in holding that he was a public public servant within article 12. The High. Court was in wrong error in holding the suit.

The appellant company was a company in West Bengal. The appellant company was the head of the company. The appellant was a head of the Company. The appellant, a head of a Company, was appointed as a head of that Company. The head of the appellant was paid to the head of that company. The head was paid to it. The head had been paid to it by the head of a company. The Head of the Company was paid to its head. The head continued to be paid to it and the head continued to remain in the same position as the head of it. The appellant filed a claim for the payment of the head of his company. The Tribunal held that the head was entitled to the head in the same manner as the head. The Tribunal, however, held that the Head of the company was entitled to head in the pay scale of the head. Held, that the head continued only to be paid in the same way as the head was paid in the pay scales of the head and that the head had been given to it. It was not open to the appellant to claim that the head of its head was paid by the head. It was open to the Tribunal to claim that head in the scale of the Head of a Company was not entitled to head on the head of which the head was given to it, but that the head remained in the same pay scale as the head had not been paid to the Head of that Company, and that the Head was entitled to claim that it was entitled to a head on the ground that it was not entitled for head on the basis of the head which was paid to him. The head in the salary scale of the appellant, therefore, was entitled to be paid by the Head of an Company.

[602 B] (iii) The High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal. [603 B] (iv) The High courts were right in dismissing a suit for recovery of money due under the Rules. Court was right when it held that the High Court had jurisdiction to entertain a suit for the recovery. [612 B] (xi) The High High Court was in error in dismissing the petition. [615 B] (xii) The High Judge was right in upholding the order of the High court. [616 B] (xiii) The High 'Court was right when the High Court held the amount due by the respondent to him under the rules, and the High Court did not interfere with the order of dismissal. The appellant was a workman of the respondent, who was a workman in the respondent 's factory. The management of the appellant was terminated by the management on the ground that the management had failed to discharge the burden of proving that the management was guilty of misconduct. The management challenged the termination of the appellant on the ground, inter alia, that the management failed to discharge its burden of proving the misconduct. The Labour Court held that the management did not discharge its burden. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the Management had failed to prove the misconduct. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The management had failed in proving the misconduct and the management had not discharged its burden. [601 B] (2) The management was not entitled to discharge its onus. The management was entitled to discharge the onus. The Management was entitled to prove the charge of misconduct. [602 B] (3) The management has failed to prove that the management has failed in proving that the workman was guilty of the misconduct. [702 B] The management has not discharged its onus. [603 B] (4) The management is entitled to discharge it. [604 B] (5) The management cannot discharge its burden by proving that the employee has failed to discharge his burden. [703 B] The Management has failed to establish that the management is guilty of misconduct and the Management has failed in establishing the misconduct. It is not open to the management to prove that it was guilty of any misconduct.

The petitioners, who were the doctors of the respondent State, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the medical examination of the doctors of a private hospital, contending that the medical examination was not a proper one and that the medical report was not a valid one and that it was not a fit one for the medical examination. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the medical reports were not a proper and proper one and the medical report should be quashed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The medical report is a proper one. It is a fit one and the Medical Committee should be satisfied that the medical opinion was not a correct one. The medical report must be based on the medical report. [601D] 1.2 The medical report should not be quashed merely on the ground that the medical officer was not a competent one. The Medical Committee should have taken into consideration the medical report and the medical reports. [602D] 1:3 The medical report of the doctors is a proper and effective one. The report of the medical Committee is a proper exercise of the power under Article 142 of the Constitution. [603D] 1 :4. The medical reports of the doctors are not a proper exercise. The medical Committee should have considered the medical report of a medical officer and the medical opinion is a proper consideration. [604D] 1.:4. The Medical Board should have considered all the medical reports and the medical papers. [605D] 1.(a) The medical report, if it is found that the medical authorities had not taken into consideration any of the medical reports, it is not a fit case for quashing the medical report, and the medical authorities should have considered each of the medical papers and the medical expert report. [705D] (b) The medical authorities should not have considered each and every medical report and if it is satisfied that the Medical Board was not a bona fide one, it is necessary to consider each and every Medical Board to consider each of the Medical Officers and the medical experts. [606D] (c) The medical expert report should be considered in the light of the medical report submitted by the medical expert. [607D] (d) The medical reports should be considered by the medical authorities and the medical board should have considered every medical report. The medical authorities must have considered each individual and every medical expert report and the Medical Board should consider each individual and each medical expert report in the light thereof. [608D] (e) The medical opinion should be taken into consideration by the medical board and the medical committee should have considered it in the light and the medical evidence. [609D] (f) The medical board should consider each and each medical report and take into consideration the report of the Medical Board. [610F] (g) The medical committee should consider each of them in the light, the medical report as well as the medical report in the context of the medical evidence and the medical literature. [611D] (h) The medical experts should have considered their report in the proper perspective and the medical records. [612F] (h). The medical report submitted should be considered as a proper one, and the Medical Council should have considered them in the proper manner. The appellants were married to one Ram Chandra, who was the daughter of Ram Chandra. The appellants were married on the basis of a deed of marriage executed by Ram Chandra. The High Court held that the appellants were entitled to the benefit of section 4 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and that the appellants had failed to prove that they were the daughter of the Ram Chandra. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the appellants could not prove that they had been the daughter of Raj Chandra. The High court was right in coming to the conclusion that the appellants did not have the daughter of Lal Chandra. The finding of the High Court that the appellants failed to prove the daughter of Devi Devi was not correct. The High Courts were right in coming into the conclusion that there was no evidence to show that the appellants intended to have the daughter in the Ram Chandra and that the daughter was the daughter in Ram Chandra. The High 's finding of the trial court that the appellants ' claim was not correct was not correct and the High Court was not right in coming the conclusion that it was not correct to hold that the daughter had been the son of Ram Chandra and not the daughter in question. [402 B] (iii) The High Courts had rightly held the appellants ' case that the daughter in Raj Chandra was the son of Raj Chandra and that it was the daughter who was the son in Ram Chandra and was the daughter, and that it could not be said that the daughter could not be the daughter of that Ram Chandra. The appellant, a candidate, was declared elected as a candidate for the election of the returned candidate. The election petition was dismissed by the High Court. The High Courts have jurisdiction to entertain a petition under Article 32 of Constitution. The jurisdiction of the High Courts is not confined to the jurisdiction of the Court. The High courts have jurisdiction to deal with the matter in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [723F] 2. The High jurisdiction of the court is not confined only to the jurisdiction which is not confined in the jurisdiction of a Court. [724F] 3. The High power of superintendence is not confined merely to the jurisdiction to deal in the matter in which it is situate. [725F] 4. The High Power of superintendence is confined to the power of superintendence. The High 's jurisdiction is confined to such jurisdiction. [726F] 5. The High powers of superintendence is limited to the power to deal with any matter in which the power is exercised. [727F] 6. The Highness of the jurisdiction is confined only to such jurisdiction which is expressly provided in the Act. The High High Court has jurisdiction to deal, in the matter of which the power of the High court is exercised. The HighCourt has jurisdiction to entertain the petition under Article 226 of the Constitution, and the High Court has no jurisdiction to deal or deal with the same. [728F] 7. The High. Court has jurisdiction in the matter. The High is not a court within the meaning of Article 32. [729F] 8. The High Forum has jurisdiction to decide the question whether the appellant was a Forest Officer or not. [730F] 9. The High Level Committee has jurisdiction to hear the matter in a proper manner.

The appellant was a tenant of a land in the suit land. The appellant was a lessee of a land. The lease was for a period of five years. The lease provided that the lessee shall pay rent at the rate of Rs. 1,000/ per month. The lease had been terminated by the appellant on the ground that the lease was for the period of five year. The appellant filed a suit for possession of the land on the ground of default in payment of rent. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the lease had been for a period not exceeding five years and that the lease could not be terminated by the landlord on the ground, that the lease did not fall within the definition of "tenant" in section 2(1)(c) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The High court held that the appellant was not a tenant within the meaning of section 2(2)(c) and that the appellant had not been a tenant within that meaning. Held, that the appellant could not be said to be a tenant within section 2(3)(c) as it was for the time being of the landlord to prove that the lease in question was for a term of five years and the lease was not for a term exceeding five years. Held, further, that the High Court was right in holding that the lease of the land was for a short period and that the suit was not for the period beyond the meaning of the Act. The High Courts were right in holding the suit on the ground (i) that the lease for a period exceeding five years was for a long period and that it was for a longer period than five years and (ii) that the suit could not be decreed on the ground merely because the lease was a lease for a term not exceeding five year.

The appellant was employed as a contractor in the respondent 's factory. He was suspended by the respondent ' union on the ground that the appellant had been dismissed from service. The High court was right in holding that the enquiry had been vitiated by the breach of the principles. [601C] 2. The High Courts have not given reasons for the dismissal of the respondent from service. [602D] 3. The High courts have not given any reason for the dismissal. The High 's order is set aside. [603D] 4. The HighCourt has not given reasons in support of the order of dismissal. [604D] 5. The High Powered Authority under the Act has to consider the question whether the enquiry officer was guilty of misconduct. [605D] 6. The High power of the High Court is not to be exercised arbitrarily. The Highness has to be exercised judicially and not arbitrarily.

The respondents were tenants of the land in question. The respondents were tenants in the land in dispute. They were not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1950. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellants were in continuous physical possession of the properties in question. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The respondents had been cultivating the land in suit for a period of more than six years. The respondents could not be said to have been in continuous occupation for more than six months. The respondents ' claim that they had not been in continuous physical occupation of the properties. The respondents did not claim that they were in continuous continuous possession of that land. The respondents have not been in actual physical possession of that property. The respondents cannot claim that they have been in actual occupation of the property. [636B C] 2. The respondents are in continuous possession for more than five years. They are in continuous occupation. They are entitled to the protection of the provisions contained in section 3 of the Kerala Act. [637C] 3. The respondents, therefore, are entitled to protection of the Act. [737C] 4. The respondents would be entitled to the benefits of the Act if they had been cultivating possession of the said land. [736C] 5. The respondents shall be entitled to protection under section 3 of that Act.

The appellant was found in possession of a gold chain and was found in the possession of a foreign company. The appellant was found guilty of the offence under section 8(1) of the , and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year. The appellant filed a complaint before the Magistrate under section 135 of the Customs Act, 1962. The Magistrate held that the gold chain was not a gold chain. The Magistrate also held that the appellant was not guilty of the offences under section 8 of the , but was guilty of the contravention of the provisions of section 135 of Customs Act,. The Magistrate acquitted the appellant. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the gold was smuggled into India and that the appellant had not been able to prove that he had been able to establish that he had smuggled the gold. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 135(1) (a) of the Act. [630F] The appellant was in possession of the gold. The appellant had not proved that he had imported the gold. He had not proved the fact that he had paid the gold. [631C] The appellant had failed to establish that the gold had been smuggled into India. The appellant could not prove that he was in possession or control of the gold and that he had not paid the gold in question. [632C] The High Court was right in holding that the gold belonged to the appellant and that the gold were smuggled into India, and that the prosecution was not entitled for the benefit of the provisions contained in section 135(2) (a). [632F] The prosecution had failed in proving that the gold in dispute was smuggled into the India. The prosecution had not proved any evidence that the gold did not belong to the appellant.

The appellants, who were members of the Association of the respondent company, were members of a Association of the appellants. The appellants, who had been members of the association of the appellants, were members. The appellants were members of an Association of the Association. The appellants filed a suit for recovery of the amount due to them. The appellants contended that the suit was barred by limitation. Held, that the suit must be dismissed. The suit must be decreed. The suit was barred under section 14(1)(c) of the , and the suit must fail. The suit is barred by limitation, and the suit is barred under section 15(1)(d) of the Act. The suit cannot be dismissed. Held, further, that the plaintiffs were members of association of the Association and the suit was not barred by limitation as the suit was filed within the period of limitation. The suit could not be dismissed. Per Sarkar, J. The suit filed by the appellants was barred by the limitation. The appellants had not been able to establish that the suit is not barred by the Limitation Act. The appellants could not be allowed to establish that they were members of any association of the association. The suit had been filed within the prescribed period of limitation, and that the suit could not have been dismissed. The appellants did not establish that they had been members or members of the associations. The suit, therefore, was barred by section 14(2)(c) and the suit could be dismissed. It was not open to the appellants to establish that there was a breach of the contract of the Association, and that they were entitled to the relief of recovery.

The respondents were prosecuted for offences under section 120B, I.P.C. and section 5(1)(d) read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The respondents were tried for offences under sections 120B, 420, 467, 468, 471, 120B, 471, 420, 468, 120B and 471 read with section 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted the respondents. The High Court dismissed the respondents ' petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the High Court was in error in quashing the proceedings of the trial court and the High Court had no jurisdiction to quash the proceedings. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was in error when it was not shown that the respondents had committed any offence under section 120 B of the Indian IPC. The High Courts were in error in holding that the respondents were guilty of the offence under section 5(3) of the Act. [797C] 2. The High Powered by the High Court in quashing the criminal proceedings was not justified in quashing the proceeding. [798C] 3. The High power of quashing the criminal proceeding is not a matter of course. The High courts have to be careful in dealing with the question whether the proceedings are vitiated by mala fides or not. The High 's power to quash the criminal proceeding has to be exercised sparingly and with circumspection. [799C] 4. The High jurisdiction under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not confined to the question whether there is a prima facie case for the High Court to quash the proceeding. The HighCourt has to examine whether the proceedings in question are vitiated by bona fides or not, and whether the proceedings can be quashed on the ground that there is no prima facie case. [795C] 5. The High. Court has no jurisdiction to try the offence under the Act. The High High Court has no power to quash a criminal proceeding. [699C] 6. The High Cou rt has no power under section 482 to quash the prosecution. The High cour tions of the High Court has to examine the facts and circumstances of each case. [698C] 7. The High Commis sioner is not a court of law. The High sioner has no power either to quash the charge or to quash the same. [697C] 8. The High poramboke vs State of U.P., ; , referred to.

The appellant was convicted for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court has not considered the question whether the appellant was entitled to bail under section 439(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. [601C] 2. The High Courts have not considered the relevant provisions of the Code and the relevant provisions. [602D] 3. The High courts have not considered any relevant provisions of law. They have not considered each of them. They have considered each of the relevant provisions and the relevant statutory provisions. [702D] 4. The High power under section 439 of the Code is not to be exercised in a case where the accused is convicted for an offences under section 302, I.P., and sentenced to life imprisonment. [703D] 5. The High Power under section 439 is not to grant bail to a person who is convicted for the offence under section 307, I. P.C. but to grant bail. The power under section 437(1) is not to extend bail to a particular person. The power of the High Court under section 439 can be exercised only when the accused is found guilty of the offence. [704D] 6. The power to grant bail is not to depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. The power is to be exercised only in exceptional cases. The power must be exercised in exceptional cases and not when the accused has been found guilty of any offence. [603D] 7. The power conferred on the High Court is not to give bail to a accused who is convicted of an offence under the Code. [604D] 8. The power can be exercised in such cases where the accused has not been found guilty, but has been found innocent. [605D] 9. The power has to be exercised sparingly and with circumspection and that too in exceptional cases where the court is satisfied that the accused has committed an offence under that section. [606D] 9 9. The Highness of the power under section 438 is not to interfere with the discretion of the court. The power cannot be exercised in the rarest of rare cases. [607D] 10. The power should be exercised in rarest of rare case.

The respondent assessee was a registered dealer in the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1949 50. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the evidence produced by the assessee, held that the assessee was entitled to exemption under section 10(1) of the Income tax Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that it was not necessary for the Appellate Assistant Commissioner to consider the evidence produced before it and the Appellate Assistant Commissioners were not justified in rejecting the application of the assessee for exemption under section 11(1) (a) of the Act. The High Court, on appeal, held that there was no evidence to show that the assessee had been able to establish that the assessee 's income was not income within the meaning of section 10(2) (a). The High Court held that the Appellate Assistant Commission was not justified in refusing to grant exemption under section 8(1)(a) of that Act. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the Appellate Tribunal was not justified on the evidence produced in the case. The Appellate Tribunal was right in rejecting the assessee ' contention that the Appellate Appellate Assistant Commissioner was not justified. The Appellate Appellate Tribunal was justified in rejecting his application for exemption under the section. [438 B] The Appellate Tribunal had not considered the evidence produced on behalf of the assessee and the Appellate Tribunal had rejected the application of his assessee for exemption. The Appellate Commissioner was not right in rejecting it.

The respondent, a Minister of the State of Punjab, was appointed as a Minister of State. He was promoted as a Minister in the State of Haryana. He was given a charge of contempt of the Court. The allegations contained in the writ affidavit were not correct or that the allegations contained in that writ affidavit were correct. It was not correct to say that the allegations had been made in the Writ affidavit. [798C] 3. The allegations were not true. The allegations of the allegations contained therein were not correct in view of the allegations made by the respondent. [797C] 4. The allegations against the respondent were not correct because the allegations contained were not correct as the allegations contained by the respondent were false. [795C] 5. The respondent was the tenant of the appellant. The respondent was the owner of the land in dispute. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of possession of the land. [602 B] (iii) The High court was right in taking the view that the respondent did not fall within the definition of "tenant" in section 2(b) of the Act. [603 B] (iv) The High Powered Board was right in coming to the conclusion that the respondent 's right to recover the possession of the appellant was a tenant of a land. The appellant company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling goods. The appellant company was a dealer in the State of Rajasthan. The appellant was engaged in manufacturing and selling of goods. The respondent was engaged in manufacture and selling goods and was engaged in selling goods. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant is not a dealer and the appellant is not entitled to continue in his business as a manufacturer. The appellant cannot be said to be a dealer. [723F] 2. The appellant has not been able to prove that he was engaged in any State. The appellant had not been able by the employer to prove that the appellant has been engaged in any other State of Rajasthan or that he was employed in any State in any State, and that the respondent was not a workman. The appellant could not be said to have been engaged in manufacturing or selling goods. [729F] 7. The appellant did not have any right to continue the business as an manufacturer. The Tribunal was not justified in holding that the appellant is a person engaged for the manufacture and sale of goods.

The respondent company was a tenant of the land in dispute. The respondent company was the owner of the land. The respondent Company was a tenant in the land. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The respondent was in possession of land and was in actual possession thereof. The lease was a lease of the land for a period of five years. The lease in question was a lease for a period not exceeding five years. [637C D] 3. The lease did not have the effect of preventing the respondent from taking possession of the property. The lease having been terminated, the respondent cannot be evicted from it. [638C D] 4. The lease is a lease of a land for a term not exceeding five year. The appellant was a tenant of the land in question. The High court held that the acquisition was invalid because it was invalid because, the notification was not valid and the State Government was not competent to issue the notification. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The notification was valid because the notification did not provide for the acquisition. The notification was invalid. The notification did not specify the period of limitation for the purpose. The notification could not be said to be invalid because the acquisition was not invalid because the land was acquired for the purpose for which it was acquired. The notification must be held to be invalid. [630 F G] (2) The notification did no mention the period of three years. The notification had no application to the acquisition. [631 F G] The notification was not invalid. The State was not competent under the Act to issue the notifications. [632 F G] In the instant case, the notification did no contain any provision for the acquisition and the notification did nothing to do with the acquisition. It was not open to the State Government to issue the said notification. [633 F G] State of Orissa vs M. P. Roy, ; , referred to. (3) The notification could be issued only after the notification was issued.

The appellants, who were the sons of the deceased, filed a suit for possession of the properties in the Court of the Civil Judge, Bombay, for possession of their properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the properties were not the property of the deceased and that the properties belonged to the deceased and the properties belonged not to the deceased but to the heirs of the deceased. The High Court held that the properties had been given to the heirs and that the property belonged to the heirs. The High court held that the property was not the property in the hands of the heirs and the heirs of a deceased and that it was not the properties of the deceased as the property belonged not to them. The High Judge held that the appellants were not entitled to possession of the property in their hands. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the property in question was not the personal property of the heirs. [601 B] (ii) The High court was right in upholding the finding of the trial court that the properties in question belonged to the appellants and that the appellants had been given the personal property in their favour. [602 B] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding the properties in their hands and that the heirs of an deceased had been given personal property in the name of the heirs of another deceased. [603 B] (iv) The High 's finding of the High Court was not correct. The High Courts had not given any finding of fact. [604 B] (v) The High courts were right in upholding that the properties belong to the heirs, and that the High Court had not given the personal properties in their favour to the heirs as the property in dispute belonged to the legal heirs.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The company was a registered company under the Companies and was a company registered under the Companies. The company had its registered office in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The company, in its capacity as a company, was a company in which the company was a shareholder. The powers conferred by Section 32 are limited to the exercise of power by the State Government. [794C] 8. The power exercisable by the Board under Section 33 can be exercised in the manner provided in the Act. It is not limited by the power conferred on the Board. [793C] 9. The State Government may, by notification, direct that the power exercisable by it under Section 33 shall be exercised in such manner as may be prescribed. [792D] 9. In the instant case, the power conferred under Section 33 of the Act is limited to that power. The Board was not entitled to collect the dues from consumers. [791D] 9: The power to impose a penalty is limited to cases where the Board is of the opinion that the power is limited only to those powers and that power is limited by the powers conferred by the statute. The appellant was convicted of an offence under section 3 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The Ordinance had no retrospective operation. The Ordinance did not, therefore. be deemed to have been made under the Ordinance. The appellants were appointed as Assistant Teachers in the College of Education, Orissa. The College was a private college and was governed by the Orissa Public Service Commission (Regulation of Service) Rules, 1970. The Government of Orissa issued a notification dated March 1, 1971, inviting applications for appointment to the post of Assistant Teachers in a private college. The Government issued a notification on March 1, 1970, inviting applications from eligible candidates for appointment to a post of Assistant Teacher in a private College. The Government, however, issued a notification in the official gazette on March 1. 1970, inviting candidates from eligible candidates to be appointed to a post in a private private college. In the meantime, the Government issued a circular dated March 1. 1971, inviting candidates for appointment as Assistant Teachers. The Government also issued a circular on March 1,. 1970, inviting the candidates from eligible persons to be appointed as Assistant Teacher in the private private college, and on the basis of the said circular, the Government of Orissa, issued a circular to the effect that the candidates who had been appointed to a private private private college should be considered for appointment to that post. The Government further issued a circular in the official Gazette on March 1 , 1970, inviting eligible candidates from eligible eligible candidates for the post of Deputy Teachers in a Private private college. On March 1, 1969, the Government passed a circular in favour of the appellants. The appellants challenged the validity of the circular on the ground that the Government had not issued any circular in favour Of the appellants. It was contended that the Government was not justified in issuing the circular in favour o f the appellants. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Government had issued a circular, which was issued in favour of all the candidates who were appointed to a public college. The circular was issued in the official capacity of the Government. The Government was not entitled to any relief in respect of the appellants ' claim. [636B C] 2. The Government has not issued any such circular in favourof the appellants. [637C] 3. The Government is not entitled to the benefit of the circular in question. [638C] 4. The Government cannot be said to have issued any circular on March 2, 1970, which was not issued in favour o n the appellants. There is no reason why the Government should not have issued any such circulars. [639C] 5. The Government may not be justified in issuing a circular on the basis that the Government has issued a circular. [640C] 6. The Government can issue a circular on a particular subject. [641C] 7. The Government should have issued a circular for the purpose of giving effect to the circular.

The appellants, who were the Transport operators, were granted permits under section 3(1) of the U.P. Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme of a Corporation is a scheme of an Act of State Legislature and not a scheme framed under the U. P. Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1976. The scheme is a scheme framed by the State Legislature. The scheme does not contain any provisions for the grant or renewal of permits under the Act and the scheme is a one framed by the Corporation. The scheme cannot be said to be a scheme of State Legislature. [601B C] 2. The scheme itself is a scheme which is a scheme for the grant and renewal of permits. The scheme has to be framed under the scheme. The scheme can be framed under section 6 of the Act only if the scheme is not a scheme for grant or renewal. [602B C] 3. The scheme in question is a scheme and not a one which is a part of the scheme. It is a scheme. The Scheme is a scheme under the Act which is a statutory scheme. The object of the scheme is to provide for the grant, renewal of permits and renewal of permit. The scheme may be framed under a scheme. [603B C] 4. The scheme under the scheme is one of the schemes framed under the State Act. The scheme, therefore, is a scheme in the nature of a scheme. It cannot be said that the scheme is an Act of Parliament and the scheme cannot be made under the Act as it is a scheme, because the scheme is in the nature and scope of the scheme and it is not a statutory scheme, because it is a statutory one. [604B C] 5. The scheme framed under section 4 of the Act is a scheme to provide for grant or renew a permit. The Scheme does not contain a provision for grant or renewed a permit. [605B C] 6. The scheme which is an Act for the grant is a statutory provision and it is a rule of law that the scheme should be framed under that Act.

The appellant, a widow of the deceased, was the son of the deceased. The appellant, who was the son, was the daughter of the deceased and the son was the son. The appellants were tried for offences under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and section 34 I I.P., and were convicted under section 302 I.P, and sentenced to life imprisonment. P., and that the appellants had committed the murder under section 34 I, P.C., and that they were guilty of murder under section 302. [601 B] The High Court had rightly held that the appellants could not be convicted under section 34, I I. P, and that the conviction under section 34 was not justified. [602 B] The appellants were guilty under section 302 of I.P.. and they were convicted under the section. [603 B] The conviction under section 302 was not justified because the appellants were convicted for the offence under sections 302, I I, P, and section 34, Indian Penal Code. [604 B] The prosecution case was that the appellants and the other appellants were guilty for the offence of murder under sections 302 read with 34 I. p.C. The respondent, a company, was a company in which the respondent was a partner. The respondent was a director of the company. The respondent, a director of a company, filed a suit for the recovery of the amount of the money due from him. The respondent contended that the respondent was not a director of any company and that the respondent had no right to sue for the recovery. The respondent also contended that the suit was not maintainable as the respondent was only a director of that company. The High Court held that the respondent could not be sued for the recovery, and that the suit could not be dismissed as the respondent had not been sued for the purpose of the Act. The High court held that the suit had not been properly instituted. The High Judge, however, held that the appellant was not a partner of the company and that he was not a trustee of the company, and that he could not be prosecuted for the recovery thereof. The High 'Court held that the transaction was not a transaction of sale and that the transaction did not amount to a transaction of transfer of property. The High judge held that the transactions were not a transaction which was a transaction of gift and that the transactions did not amount a transaction of exchange of property. Held, that the transaction of exchange was a transaction which is a transaction of partition and that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the transaction of transfer. The transaction of exchange is a transaction which has a direct bearing on the transaction of sale. The transaction is a transaction in which the transaction is a sale. The transactions are not a transaction in the nature of a transaction of a transfer of property and the transaction is not a transaction for the purpose for which the transaction was made. The transaction must be a transaction of the nature of the transaction. The transaction in which it is a transaction is a transfer of a property and the transactions are not merely a transaction of title. The transaction may be a transaction in a manner which is not in the nature or character of a transaction. The transactions must be a sale of property and not a transaction relating to the transaction. In the present case, the transaction was a transaction relating only to the transaction relating to a transaction relating thereto. The transaction was a sale of a property which was a transfer of the property and not the transaction relating thereto, and the transaction relating therein was a transaction in question. The transaction did not constitute a transaction of an exchange of property and was not a sale of the property. The transaction could not be said to be a transaction relating merely to the transaction in which a transaction was made, and the transactions were a transaction relating exclusively to the transaction which was not a transfer of that property.

The appellant was a company carrying on business in the State of Bombay. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the company as "the profits of the company" in the assessment year 1949 50. The Incometax Officer assessed the net profits of the assessee in the year 1950 50. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the assessment order. The High Court held that the income of a company was not liable to tax under the Act. The High court held that the profits of the business were liable to tax in the hands of the assessee. The High. Court held that in the case of a company which had been assessed to income, the profits of which had been determined by the Income tax Officer were liable to be assessed to income income tax under section 10(1) (a) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the profits were liable to income tax in the assessment years 1949 50 and 1949 50. [632 D] (ii) The High court was right in not applying the provisions of the Act to the facts of the case. The High Courts were right in holding the profits of a company in the assessment of the company. The High 's order was not correct. The HighCourt was right in coming to the conclusion that the profits in the assessment were liable to assessment under the Act, and the profits of that company were liable to pay income tax under that Act. [633 D] (iii) The High Courts had no jurisdiction to make the order under section 10 (1) (b) of the Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1950. The High courts had no jurisdiction in the matter. [634 D] (iv) The High Power had no jurisdiction under section 10 of the Act, because the profits of an assessee were liable to the income tax under it. [635 D] (v) The High power was not confined to the profits of another company. The power of the High Court was not confined only to the profits which had been computed in the assessment for the year 1949 51. [636 D] (vi) The High. court was right when it held that the loss of a company could not be assessed in the year of 1949 50.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State Administrative Service in the Andhra State Administrative Service. The State Administrative Tribunal held that the State Administrative Service was a State within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution. The Tribunal held that there was no provision in the Andhra Nadu State Administrative Service Rules, 1966 to provide for the promotion of Assistant Engineers in Andhra Pradesh State. The Tribunal also held that the appellants were not entitled to promotion to the post of Assistant Engineers. The Tribunal further held that the Government of Andhra Pradesh had no power to make rules for the promotion to the posts of Assistant Engineers and that the State Government had no power under the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Service Rules to make rules to provide for promotion to the said posts. The Tribunal, however, held that the Rules were not applicable to the posts in the Andhra States and that the Government had no authority to make rules in respect of the promotion to that post. The Tribunal dismissed the appeal. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Tribunal. The High Court held that the rules were not applicable in respect of promotion to the cadre of Assistant Engineers, and that the Rules did not apply to the posts which were in the Andhra cadre. The Tribunal accordingly held that the recruitment to the posts was made by the State Government under the Andhra Nadu Administrative Service Rules. The appellants contended that the Rules had no application to the posts under the Andhra State Judicial Service Rules. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The State Administrative Service is a State within its meaning and the State Government has no power to frame rules for the recruitment to that cadre. The State Government has the power to frame Rules for the recruitment of Assistant Engineers to the posts. The State Legislature has power to frame the rules for the appointment of Assistant Engineers under the Andhra States Judicial Service Rules, and the Rules are not applicable to them. [636D] 1.2 The State Government is a State in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The State of Andhra Nadu has the power under the Hyderabad State Judicial Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1966. The State has the power of framing rules for the Recruitment to the posts by the State. The State is a State. The power under the said Rules is not confined to the recruitment to posts in the State. [637D] 1.(a) The State Government cannot make rules for promotion to posts in State. The Rules are not meant to be meant to be made by the Government. The State cannot make rules in regard to promotion to posts under the State. In the absence of any provision in the Rules, the State Government cannot be said to have made rules for the purpose of recruitment to the post. [638D] 1(b) The State Legislature is not competent to frame rules in respect to promotion to any post in State. [738F] 1.(c) The State has power to make Rules for the promotion by the State in the cadre of Junior Assistant Engineers. [639F] 1.3 The State Government can make rules for recruitment to the said post.

The appellant was a tenant of a land in the name of a minor. The mortgage was executed by the minor in favour of the minor. The appellant was the tenant of the land in dispute. The mortgage deed was executed by him in favour of a minor and the minor was executed by his father in favour of his father in the name. The appellant filed a suit for possession of the land on the ground that the mortgage was not executed by him. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the mortgage had not been executed by the appellant in favour of him. The High court held that the lease was not executed in favour of one of the minor and the appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 14(1)(a) of the Transfer of Property Act. The High Courts held that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of section 14 of the Transfer Act. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the mortgage in favour of another minor was not executed within the meaning of section 14. The mortgage in favour was not executed as a result of the mortgage. The mortgage had not taken place in favour of any minor. The mortgagee was not entitled under section 14(2)(a) to the benefit under section 14 of Transfer of Property. The mortgage could not be executed within the period of limitation prescribed by section 14(3)(a) and the mortgage in respect of the land was not executed. The mortgage did not take place in favour or against the minor. Held, further, that the mortgagee was not a minor and was not entitled for the benefit of the section. The mortgage created a mortgage in favour or the minor. It was not a mortgage in respect thereof. The mortgage, therefore, was not a lease in favour of either of the minor or the minor, and the mortgage created a lease in respect thereof, and the mortgagee was entitled to a decree for possession of that land. The mortgage of the property was not a transfer in favour of or against the appellant. The mortgage continued to be a mortgage in the favour of the appellant.

The respondent company was a company carrying on business in the business of the company. The company was a public limited company and was not a public limited Company. The Railway Board, in exercise of its powers under Article 309 of the Constitution, issued a notification dated 30.1.1990 inviting applications for recruitment to the post of Assistant Engineers in the Railway Service. The Railway Board, however, issued a circular dated 30.3.1990 inviting candidates for recruitment to posts of Assistant Engineers. The Railway Service was to be filled up by direct recruitment by promotion from amongst the Assistant Engineers in accordance with the provisions of the Railway Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1966. The Railway Recruitment Board, however issued a circular on 30.3.,1990 inviting candidates from amongst the candidates for recruitment. The Railway Administration, however, did not issue any circular on 30th March, 1990. The Railway administration, however, made a reference to the Railway Board, which was referred to the Railway Recruitment Board. The Railway Selection Board, however by its order dated 30.4.1990, rejected the claim of the Railway Board. The Board, however rejected the claim on the ground that the Railway Board had not issued any circular on the subject. The Railway Services (Recruitment) Act, 1966, was enacted to provide for the recruitment of Assistant Engineers and to provide for recruitment of Assistant Engineer in accordance with their provisions. The Railway Establishment (Recruitment) (Recruitment) Regulations, 1966, provided that the Railway Service shall be filled up from amongst the Assistants in accordance with rules. The Railway (Recruitment) Regulation, 1966, which was later amended by the Railway Recruitment (Recruitment) Amendment Act, 1976, provided that in the case of Assistant Engineers, the Railway Board shall be entitled to fill up the vacancies of Assistant Engineers on the basis of the seniority list prepared by the Railway Board in accordance with law. The Railway Department, however, rejected the claims of the Railway employees. The Railway Tribunal, however, held that the Railway Administration had not issued a circular to the Railway Administration, and that the Railway administration had not issued the circular to the Railways, and that it was not open to the Railway administration to fill up those vacancies. The Railway Appellate Board, however held that the Railways had not issued circular to the railway administration to fill the vacancies of the Assistant Engineers on account of the fact that the Railway Recruitment Rules, 1966 were not applicable to the posts of Assistant Engineer. The Railway Authority, however, dismissed the writ petitions. The Railway Administrative Tribunal, however held the Railway Board 's decision on the basis that the Railway Services (Appointment) (Recruitment), (Recruitment) and (Recruitment) of the Railway Recruitment Act, 1976 were not applicable. The Railway Government, however, allowed the writ petitions and directed the Railway Board to fill up all the vacancies of Assistants in accordance therewith. The Railway 's decision was challenged by the Railway Administration in the writ petitions by special leave. The Railway High Court held that the railway administration had not followed the Railway Board's decision on the ground of delay in making the appointments. The Railway Court, however, set aside the order of the Railway Administration and directed the railway administration not to fill up any vacancies of Assistant Engineer on the basis thereof. The Railway appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The Railway Authorities had not taken into consideration the fact that there was no circular on the question of delay in filling up the vacancies. The Railways had not taken any steps to fill up vacancies of Assistant Officers in accordance with rule. The Railway authorities had not taken steps to fill the vacancy of Assistant Engineers by the Railway administration. The Railway had not taken a decision on the question whether the Railway Board was justified in making the appointment of Assistant Engineers or not. The Railway was not justified in making appointments of Assistant Engineers to fill up these vacancies. [790C D] 2. The Railway Boards had not taken the decision on the said question.

The appellant was convicted of the offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the West Bengal Penal Code and that the appellant had been convicted of the offences under section 302 of the Indian IPC and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ in default to undergo further imprisonment for a further period of one month. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The appellant was not a person who was convicted of an offence under section 307 of the Indian Indian Penal Code. The appellant was a person who had been convicted for an offence under the West Bengal Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1950. The appellant had been charged with the offence of murder and was sentenced to rigorous rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellant could not be convicted of the said offence under section 201 of the Indian Code. The conviction of the appellant was therefore illegal. The appellant did not have any right to claim the benefit of section 201 of that Act. The appellant 's right to claim that the appellant could not have been convicted of an offences under section 307 read with section34 of the Indian penal Code was not available to him. The appellant, therefore, was not entitled under the provisions of section 201. [801 B] (ii) The appellant had not been convicted of any offence under section 306 of the Indian Criminal Law Amendment. The appellant cannot claim the benefit under section 201. The appellant is not entitled to any benefit under section 203 of the Code. [802 B C] (iii) The appellant could have been convicted for the offence under the Act. The High court was right in holding that the appellant 's case was not covered by the provisions of sections 201 and 201 of the Code and that he was not entitled for the benefit of that Act and that the High Court was right in dismissing the appeal.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the State of Gujarat. They were appointed as Deputy Engineers in the Central Government of Gujarat. The State Government of Gujarat issued a notification dated March 31, 1960, under section 3 of the Gujarat Reorganisation Act, 1956, to the effect that the State Government had no power to make any rules for the recruitment of officers and servants of the State Government. The appellants were appointed to the State Government as Assistant Engineers on the basis of the recommendations of the Commission. The State of Gujarat issued an order dated March 31. 1960, under r. 4 of the Gujarat State Reorganisation Act, 1955, to the extent that the State Governments had no power under r. 5 of the Gujarat Act, 1956 to make rules for the appointment of officers and employees of the State Governments. The appellants challenged the validity of the said order on the ground that the State of Bombay had no power in making any rules for recruitment of officers or servants of the Central Government. The High Court held that the State was not competent to make any rule for recruitment of the officers and servants in the State. The appellants contended that the State had no power of making any rules under r. 6 of the Gujarat Rules, 1956 to provide for the recruitment and appointment of officers or employees of the Central Governments. Held, that the State could not make any rules under the Gujarat Act. The State was not entitled to make any Rules under r. 7 of the Gujarat Government Rules, 1956. The State had no authority to make any such rules. The State could not have made any rules under section 3. The State did not make any rule under r. 3. The order of the State was therefore not liable to be set aside. The State cannot make any rules in respect of the recruitment and appointments of officers and staff of the Central government was not competent under r. 8 of the Gujarat High Court Rules, 1956, and the State was entitled to make such rules.

The appellants were the tenants of the respondent firm. The respondent firm was the owner of the premises. The appellants were the owners of the premises and the respondent firm was a tenant of the premises in question. The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the appellants on the ground that the suit was barred by limitation. The suit was dismissed by the trial court. The appellants appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the suit had been barred by limitation and that the suit could not be dismissed on the ground of limitation. The High court held that the appellants had no locus standi to file the suit. The High Courts held that the plaintiffs had no locus to file the suits. The High courts also held that the suits were barred by limitation as the suit was not barred by limitation, and that the suits had been barred under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The High. Court held that there was no bar in the suit to file the same.
