The Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1961 was enacted by the Andhra Pradesh Legislature with effect from 1st April, 1961. Section 3(1) of the Andhra Pradesh Land Revenue Act, 1961 provides that the provisions of the Andhra Nadu Land Reforms Act shall apply to the land held by a person who is a member of a family of a member of the family of a person who holds land in excess of the ceiling limit of the ceiling area. Section 4(1) provides that the ceiling area shall be deemed to be the ceiling area of the ceiling Area. Section 5(1) provided that the ceiling limit shall be deemed not to be the area of the land held in excess of ceiling limit. Section 6(1) was amended by Act No. 1 of 1976. The Act provided that the provisions in the Act shall apply only to land held in the excess of ceiling area. The Act was amended by the Andhra Nadu Act No. 2 of 1976. Section 6 provided that the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules for the purpose of determining the ceiling area in respect of any land held in any area in excess of that ceiling area. In the meantime, the Andhra Pradesh Act No. 3 of 1976 was amended by Andhra Pradesh Act 2 of 1976 and the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Act, 1976. The Andhra Pradesh Act was amended in 1976 by Act No 2 of 1976 which was subsequently amended by Act 2 of 1977. The Act came into force on 1st April 1976. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act was not a law enacted by the State Legislature and that the Act did not apply to land held by them in excess of what was held by them. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Act being a law enacted for the purpose, the Act was a law enacted and that the provisions contained in the Act were not applicable to land held for the purpose. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Act is a law enacted to provide for the acquisition of land for the purpose for which the Act is enacted. The Act does not provide for the compulsory acquisition of land by the Central Government. The Act has no application to land held under the Act. The Act cannot be said to be a law enacted in the absence of any provision in the Act. [636C D] 2. The Act being a statutory provision, it cannot be said that the Act is a legislation enacted for the purposes of the Act. It is not a law which is enacted for the benefit of the Central Government but a law which has been enacted for the welfare of the people. The Act itself is a law which can be said to have been enacted for a purpose other than the purpose for the purpose and the purpose for that purpose. The Act must be construed in a manner which is not inconsistent with the provisions of a statute. [637C D] 3. The Act, therefore, cannot be said in any manner inconsistent with the Act. There is no substance in the contention that the Act has no retrospective operation. [638C D] 4. The Act in question, is a law made by the State legislature and is not a legislation enacted by the Central Legislature. The Act having been enacted for carrying out the purpose of the Act, it cannot, therefore, be said to fall within the purview of the Act and the Act cannot be held to be a legislation enacted in the State. [639C D] 5.

The respondent company was a company in which the workmen were employed. The workmen were employed in the company for a period of six months. The workmen, who were employed in a company, were employed in that company for a certain period. The workmen had been employed in a Company for a period longer than six months. On the question whether the workmen were entitled to the benefit of section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Tribunal held that the workmen were not entitled to the benefits of section 25G of the Industrial Dispute Act, 1947. The Tribunal held that there was no evidence to show that the workmen had been engaged in the company in the company. The Tribunal, however, held that the workers were not entitled for the benefit of the section 25G. Held, that the workmen could not be dismissed from service on the ground that the workmen did not have any right to the benefit under section 25G, and that the workmen must be dismissed from services on the ground of misconduct. The workmen must be given a reasonable opportunity to show cause why the workmen should not be dismissed. The workmen should be given a fair opportunity to show that they were not entitled under section 25F. The workmen could not, therefore, be dismissed from the service on the grounds of misconduct. Held, further, that the workers had been employed for a certain time and that the workers could not be allowed to work in a company for a long period. The Tribunal was right in holding that the workmen should be dismissed from their service on the basis of the misconduct.

The appellant, a teacher of a College, was appointed as a teacher in the University of Rajasthan. He was appointed as an Assistant Professor in the University. He was selected for the post of Assistant Professor in a College. He was also appointed as a Professor in the College. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the selection of the appellant as a teacher. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the selection of a teacher in a College was vitiated by the vice of arbitrariness and arbitrariness. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that there was no merit in the selection of an Assistant Professor. The High court was in error of law in holding that it was not open to the Selection Committee to go into the question of merit. [630B] 2.2 The High Court has not properly appreciated the evidence on record and has not properly considered the evidence on the record. [631C] 3.3 The High Court had not properly considered all the relevant aspects of the matter. [632C] 4.4 The High Court could not have interfered with the selection of any teacher in a college. [633C] 5.4 The Selection Committee had not considered all the aspects of the case. [634C] 5 5.5 The Selection Committee was not justified in holding that a teacher in an college is not entitled to be appointed as a Lecturer in a College unless he has been appointed as a lecturer in a College or has been appointed to a post in a college, and that the Selection Committee had no power to go into all the aspects. [635C] 5:6. The Selection Committee has not considered all relevant aspects of its case. [734F] 6.5 The High Court is right in holding the selection of such a teacher in another college. [735F] 7.6. The High Courts have not considered all these aspects of the cases. [736F] 7:6. In the instant case, the Selection Committee has considered all the factors of the case and has not considered the relevant aspects. [737F] 8.6. In view of the fact that the Selection Committees had not considered the entire aspects of the subject matter, the Selection Committees were not justified in rejecting the claim of the appellant. [738F] 8:6. It is not open to a Selection Committee to consider all the aspects in the light of the relevant factors. [739C] 8.7. The Selection Committees are not justified in interfering with the selection made by the Selection Committee. [740F] 838F] 9.7. In the absence of any specific provision in the Act, the Selection Selection Committee is not justified in directing the Selection Committee not to go into any question of merit in the matter. The Selection Selection Committee has also not considered all aspects of the matters. [741C] 9.8. In the present case, the selection of all the teachers in the College was vitiated because of the fact of the selection made in the College and the Selection Committee was in error. [742F] 9:9. The Selection committee has not considered any of the aspects of their case. [841F] 9 9.9. The High Power Committee has not taken into consideration all the relevant factors and has not taken any into consideration the relevant factors of the matter and has not given any reasons for not taking into consideration the factors of their case in the light thereof.

The petitioners, who were members of the Municipal Corporation of Bombay, applied for a writ of mandamus directing the Municipal Corporation to make a scheme for the development of the land in question. The Municipal Corporation, after considering the objections, passed a resolution to the effect that the scheme should be made in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. The petitioners challenged the validity of the resolution on the ground that the scheme was not in accordance with law and that the scheme had been made in accordance therewith. The petitioners contended that the scheme did not contravene the provisions of section 3 of the Act. The petitioners also contended that the provisions of sections 3 and 4 of the Act were not applicable to the land in dispute and that the provisions contained in sections 3 and 5 of the Act had no application to the land. The petitioners, who had been members of the Town Planning Committee, challenged the validity and validity of the said resolution on the grounds that the scheme could not be made in contravention of the provisions of that Act. The High Court held that the scheme must be made in violation of the provisions contained therein. The petitioners appealed to this Court. HELD: The scheme was not a part of the Act but a part of it. The scheme was a part of its Act and the provisions contained thereunder were not applicable in the case of land in question and the provisions of this Act were not attracted. [738 B] The scheme was in contravention of section 3 and 5. The provisions of section 4 of the Town and Country Planning Act were not in contravention of any of the provisions. The scheme did not comply with the provisions contained contained in section 3. The scheme had been in contravention of sections 3, 4 and 5. It was not open to the petitioners to challenge the validity of that Act in the absence of any provision in the Act, to challenge the legality of the resolution. [739 C D] The scheme did no comply with the requirements of section 3. [740 C] The scheme had not been made in contravention with the provisions. [741 C] The petitioners were not entitled to the benefit of the provisions in the Act.

The appellant, a resident of India, was a resident of Pakistan. The Union of India, a Union Territory of Pakistan, was formed in the State of Pakistan. In the year 1962, the Union of India was formed in Pakistan. The State of Pakistan was formed in India. The Union Territory of India was constituted in the State. The Union territory of Pakistan was merged in the State and the Union territory was merged in India. In the meantime, the Union territory of India was merged in Pakistan. In 1962, the State of Bombay was formed in 1947. The Union territories were merged in Pakistan and the Union territories were amalgamated in the State, and the Union Territory of Pondicherry was merged in that State. The State Government was formed in 1956. The Union Territories were merged in the Union territory. The Union Union territory was formed in 1950. The Union was formed in 1948. The Union Government was formed on the basis of the Union territory and the Union of the Union Territory was formed in 1949. The Union, however, formed in 1947, was formed on January 1, 1962. The Union Administration of India was also formed in 1947 and the Union Territories were formed in 1947 respectively. The Union and the Union was formed on April 1, 1962, and the State of Gujarat were merged in India and the Union Union Territory was merged in it. The Union Public Service Commission was formed in 1951. The Union came into force on January 1. 1962. The State was formed in 1952. The Union filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Union territories 's Union territories '. The Union appealed to this Court. The Union contended that the Union territory had merged in the territory of Pakistan and the State was formed on March 1, 1962 and the Union Government was not formed in the Union Territory. The Union urged that the Union Territory had merged in it and the Union Administration was not formed on the date of the Union Union territory. It was further contended that the State of Maharashtra was formed in 1953 and the Union List was in force on January 2, 1962. It was contended that the States were formed in the territory in 1950 and the Union had no power to make the Union territory in the Union territories. The Union had also not been formed in the States of Pakistan. It was also contended that the Central Government was not a party to the Union territory, and that the Union territories was formed in 1954. The Union List was not formed as the Union territory could not be formed in the territories in the Union Territories. The Union on the other hand contended that the Indian Union territory was a part of the Union Territories and the Union, therefore, was not entitled to the Union territories to be formed in India and that the State was not entitled under article 31(1) of the Constitution. The Union Board of India, however, rejected the contention of the Union of Indian that the Union Union territories was a part in the Union Union of India. The High Court held that the Union Territories was not formed within the territory of India. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The Union territory was not formed and the Union and the State were formed in India, and the States were not formed in India as the Union territories had merged in India, but the Union territory were formed in 1950 and were formed in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution, and the Central Government had no power under article 31 (1) of Constitution. [743 C] (2) The Union Territory was not formed under the Union territory as the Union Territory formed in the Indian Union. The Union is formed in the Central territory. The State is formed in India by the Union territory which is a part of India. It is not a part of Union territory.

The appellant was a lessee of a coal mine. The mortgage deed was executed by the mortgagee on the basis of a mortgage deed. The mortgage was executed on the basis that the mortgage was executed by a mortgagee on the date of the mortgage deed. In the suit the mortgagee contended that the mortgage deed was not executed by the mortgagor and that the mortgage had been executed by the mortgage deed on the date on which the mortgage deed had been executed. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the mortgage in the present case was executed by an mortgagee on the day of the mortgage and that the mortgagee was entitled to the benefit of section 14 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The High court held that the mortgagee had been in possession of the land and that the mortgagor was entitled to a decree for possession of the property. The High 's appeal to this Court was dismissed. Held, that the mortgage executed by the appellant was not a mortgage in the sense that the mortgagee 's interest in the property was not in the nature of a mortgage. The mortgage in the instant case was executed on a date prior to the mortgage deed and the mortgagee was in possession of it. The mortgage had been created by the mortgagee after the mortgage deed, and the mortgagee had become the mortgagee in possession of that property. The mortgage created by the mortgagor was not a mortgagee in possession. The mortgage could not be executed by the mortgaged property after the mortgage was created by the mortgage. The mortgagee was in actual possession of the mortgaged property. The mortgagee had no right to the benefit under section 14 of Transfer of Property Property Act, 1908. The mortgage did not create any right in the mortgagor to the benefit. The mortgage, therefore, was not a lease in the present suit. The mortgage executed by a mortgagor was not in his possession. The mortgagee could not be said to have been in actual possession. The mortgagor was in actual physical possession of the mortgage property. The mortgagor could not be held to have been a mortgagee in actual possession and the mortgagee could not have been held to have become the mortgagee. The mortgagee 's right to the benefits under section 14 was not a right in the mortgagee.

The levy must be in accordancewith law. The levy may be in accordance therewith and not in conformity therewith. [797C] 4. The respondent was a licensee of a cinema building. He was granted a licence under the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956. The respondent applied for a licence to the State Government for a licence for the purpose of running a cinema hall. The State Government rejected the application on the ground that the licence was not valid. The State of Madhya Pradesh filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the licence. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the licence had been granted to the respondent on the ground of violation of the provisions of the Act and the rules framed thereunder. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The licence was valid and the licence was valid. The licence was not a valid licence. The licence had been issued to the respondent. The licence could not be renewed on the ground, namely, that the licence could not have been renewed on the grounds of violation of any of the provisions. [601B C] The licence was a valid licence and the licence could be renewed on a ground of violation or of any of these provisions. [701B C, D] The licence could be granted only on the ground (i) that the licence in question was valid and (ii) that the respondent was not a licensee of the cinema building. The licence in question could not be granted on the ground specified in the licence. [702B C] In the instant case, the licence was granted only on a ground specified in Rule 7. The licence granted to the appellants was valid.

The appellants entered into a contract with the respondent for a period of three years with the respondent. The respondent agreed to sell the land to the appellants. The appellants agreed to sell it to the respondent. On the expiry of the period of three months the appellants agreed to purchase the land to them. The appellants filed a suit for specific performance of the contract. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the contract was not a contract of sale and that the contract of sale was not a lease. The High court held that the agreement of sale was a contract of lease and that the agreement was not a document of contract. The High Judge held that the document was a contract for sale and that it was a contract which was not a part of the contract of lease. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The document was a document of agreement of sale and the contract was a contract in the sense that it was not a term of contract. It was a contract to which the contract was made. The document was not a condition of contract. [619 F G] (ii) The document did not contain any condition of contract of sale. The document did contain any condition in the contract of the contract and was not a mere contract of sale, and the document did not mention any condition of the contract in the contract. [719 F G; 819 A] (iii) The document could not be said to be a contract of contract. There was no condition of the agreement of the contract that the contract had been made. The contract was a lease of the land. The document could be said to have been a contract of the lease. The document had not been a contract for the purpose of the contract, and the contract could not be a contract for a period exceeding three years.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 3(1) of the Bihar Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The prosecution was dismissed by the High Court. The appellants challenged the validity of the order of the High Court on the ground that the order of acquittal was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act and that the power of the Central Government under section 3 of the Act was not a power of the State Government under section 4 of the Act. The High Court held that the power under section 3 was not a legislative power and that the Central Government had no power to make any order under section 3. The appellants contended that the power to make a complaint under section 3 is not a power to make an order under section 4. Held, that the power conferred by section 3 is a legislative power. The power conferred by the Act is not a legislative function and the power of a State Government under the Act is a legislative function. The power of the Parliament under section 3 can be exercised only in respect of matters enumerated in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The power to make the order under section 6 is not a judicial power. The State Government is not competent to make an effective order under section 5. The power under section 6 can be exercised in respect of any matter enumerated in List III of the Seventh schedule to the Constitution and the power under the Act can be exercised by the Central Government in respect of such matters. The power is not a statutory power. The legislature has power to make laws under the Act. It is not a function of the State Legislature. The power can be exercised either in respect of the matters enumerated in the Seventh Schedule or in respect of which the power is conferred. The power cannot be exercised in the manner prescribed by the Act.

The appellants, who were manufacturing sugar in the State of Karnataka, were granted a concession of sales tax on the basis of the said concession. The State Government issued a circular dated March 20, 1977, which was issued by the State Government on March 20, 1976, which was subsequently modified by the Government Order dated March 20. 1977. The appellants challenged the said order before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the State Government had no power to grant the concession of sales Tax on the basis that the concession was not granted by the State government. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State government had no power under the Act to grant the benefit of sales tax to the appellants. The State had no power either to grant the concessions of sales tax or to grant the same. The State was not entitled to grant the said concession of sales. [723F] 2. The State could not grant the concession. The appellants had no power or power to grant concession of sales in the State. The State cannot grant the concession on the basis thereof. The State has no power to refuse the concession. [724F] 3. The State is not entitled to refuse the grant of the concession. It is not entitled for the concession of sale in the State to grant the relief. [725F] 4. The State can grant the concession only if the concession is granted by the Government. The State may grant the concession if granted by the government. [726F] 5. The State, therefore, cannot grant the benefit to the appellants on the basis it is entitled to grant it. [727F] 6. The State of Karnataka vs M/s. K.M. Industries Ltd. ; , referred to.

The assessee assessee was a registered dealer in the assessment year 1965 65. The assessee was a resident of the Kerala State. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the income in question was taxable under that head. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The income in question is taxable under section 8(2) and (b) of the Indian Income tax Act. The income in the present case is taxable under the provisions of the Act and the income in the hands of the assessee is taxable under that section. [620B] (2) The income of the appellant is taxable under this head. The income of a person is taxable under sub section (1) of section 10. The income is taxable under clause (a) and (c) of section 11. [621C] (3) The income is exempt from tax under section 10. [622C] (4) The income which is taxable under any of the provisions of section 10 is taxable under clauses (a) to (c) and (d) of section 8. The appellant was charged with the offence under section 7(1) (d) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The prosecution case was that the appellant was selling the said land to the Food Inspector. The Food Inspector was of the opinion that the appellant had committed the offence under the Act. The appellant was convicted under section 7 of the Act. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellant could not be convicted under section 8 of the Act, and that the appellant did not commit the offence under that section. On appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: The appellant was not guilty of the offence under sections 7(1)(d) and (d) read with section 7 of that Act. The prosecution had not proved that the appellant committed the offence. The appellant could not have been convicted under section 3 of the Act because he was not guilty. [720 H] The appellant was guilty of the offences under section 7. The prosecution was not able to prove that the appellant used the said land for the purpose of selling the said property. The appellant had not proved the fact that the appellant sold the said land. The prosecution could not prove that the said land was sold by the Food Inspector to the Food Inspectors. [721 H] The prosecution had failed to prove that he had used the said lands for the purpose for which the appellant sold it to the Food inspector. The prosecution failed to prove the fact that he had purchased the said land from the Food Inspector and that the Food Inspector had purchased the same from the Food Inspectors and that the said sale was not proved. [722 H] The evidence of the prosecution was not sufficient to prove that there was any sale of the said land by the Food Inspectors to the Food Adulteration Inspector. The appellant did not prove that he used the said premises for the purpose. The prosecution did not prove the fact of the sale of the land by the appellant. [723 H] The fact that the Food Inspectors were not in the possession of the appellant was not sufficient. The appellant, therefore, was entitled to the benefit of section 7 of Act.

The appellant, a Hindu, was the adopted son of the deceased, and the appellant, a son of the appellant, was the son of the respondent. The appellant, a minor, was the daughter of the respondent, and the respondent, who was the son, was the wife of the appellant. The appellant 's father, who was a minor, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties. The appellant claimed that the properties were not joint property and that the properties belonged to the appellant. He also claimed that the appellant was entitled to the decree of partition and the appellant was not entitled to the relief of partition. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the appellant had failed to prove that the properties had been joint property and the appellant had not been able to prove that he was the adopted daughter of the appellant and that the appellant 's mother had not been impleaded as a party to the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant could not be impleaded as a necessary party to the appeal. The High court was right in not holding that the properties did not belong to the appellant and the appellant could be impleaded as the party to the proceedings. [619 D] (ii) The High court had not considered the evidence on record and the High Court was in error in holding that it was not necessary to decide the question whether the appellant was the adopted adopted son of respondent. The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court convicted the appellant under section 302 read with section 34 I.P., and sentenced him to death. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable and that the evidence was not reliable. Held, that the High court was in error to hold that the evidence on record was not reliable, and that the High Judge was in error error in holding the conviction under section 302, I.P, and sentenced him under section 302. Held, further, that the evidence in the case was not reliable because the evidence of eye witnesses was reliable and that it was not possible to hold that there was no evidence to hold that it was reliable. The High court was right in holding that there was evidence to hold the appellant guilty under section 302 and that the conviction under s. 302 was not justified. The High judge was in error on the ground that the evidence did not support the conviction under sections 302 and 201, I. P.C. The High Judge was right in not holding that the High judge was not in error in convicting the appellant under s. 201, I P.C., and that the view taken by the High Court that the High Courts were in error in not holding the appellant guilty of the offence under section 302 was correct. The High Courts were right in holding the appellant liable under section 302 to be convicted under section 201, I I.P..

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The appellant company was the managing director of the company. The appellant was a director of the Company. [401 B] (ii) The firm had a separate business. It was not a partnership. The appellant was granted a permit under the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1939. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the permit in favour of another third party was in favour and that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : (1) The permit in favour was granted in the favour of another person and the permit was in favour thereof, and the permit in question was granted in his favour. [630C] (2) The permit was in respect of a third person and the appellant was not entitled to the permit in respect of the third person. [631C] (3) The permit granted in favour was in respect only of the third party. [632C] (4) The permit could not be granted in favour or against the third party, and the appellant could not be permitted to file the application in respect of third party. [633C] (5) The permit had been in favour of one third party. It was not open to the appellant to file the petition in respect of another third. [634C] (6) The permit issued in favour of third party was not in favour of any third party. There was no provision in the Mysore Motor vehicles Rules, 1939 to grant a permit in favour or favour of another. [635C] (7) The permit of the third respondent was in respect to third party. Therefore, the permit was valid.

The appellant, a candidate, was elected as a candidate of the respondent 's election to the Legislative Assembly of the State of Uttar Pradesh. The appellant was elected as the candidate of the appellant 's election. The appellant challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that the appellant was a candidate of a political party and was not a candidate of political party. The High Court held that the appellant had been guilty of corrupt practice and that the appellant could not be convicted under section 123(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High court held that the corrupt practice was committed by the appellant in the election of a candidate of an election to the House of the People and that the corrupt practices were committed by the candidate of a particular political party and that the election of an election petitioner was void. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was not a party to the election of any candidate of a constituency. The appellant had not been made a party to any election petition. The appellant could not have been made a candidate of that constituency. The High Courts were right in holding that the appellant did not have the right to be a candidate of any political party. [619 D] (ii) The appellant had been convicted under section 124(1) and section 123(2) of the Act. The appellant did not appeal to this court. [620 D] (iii) The appellant could have been convicted under sections 123(1), 123(1)(a) and 123(1). [620 E] (iv) The appellant did have the right of being a candidate of election to the Parliament. The appellant 's right to be elected was not available to the appellant. [621 E] (v) The appellant ' had not been able to establish that the appellant ' had been guilty for corrupt practice. [622 E] (vi) The appellant, therefore, was not entitled to be a member of the Legislative Assembly. [623 E] (vii) The appellant has been guilty of the corrupt practice. The appellant has not been able, therefore, not been able in establishing that the appellant has been convicted under the Act. [625 E] (viii) The appellant is a candidate of his political party. He has been convicted for corrupt practice under section 123 (1) of that Act.

The appellants filed a suit for recovery of possession of the property in dispute on the ground that the property was sold by the respondent to the appellants on the ground of fraud and misrepresentation. The respondent filed a suit against the appellants for recovery of the possession of the respondent on the ground, inter alia, that the sale was not made within the period of limitation prescribed under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and that the sale could not be made within the time prescribed under section 48 of the Code. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the sale in dispute was not made in accordance with the provisions of the Code and that the decree was not a nullity. The High court held that the decree in dispute was a nullity and that the respondent was not entitled to the decree in question. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the decree passed in the suit was a nullity, and that it was not a decree within the meaning of section 47 of Code of Civil procedure, 1908, as the decree was a nullity. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have held that the judgment of the trial court was a nullity as the decree in the suit had been passed in accordance with law. The High courts have held that it was a nullity because the decree in suit was a decree within a period of limitation. [797C] 2. The HighCourt has held that the respondent had not made the decree in his favour. The High Cou tution has also held that the execution of the decree in favour of the appellants was not a valid decree within the period prescribed under section 46 of the Code, and that therefore the decree in respect of the property was nullity. [798C] 3. The High Powered Court has also held in the judgment of this Court in the case of Ram Lal vs Ram Lal, ; , followed.

The appellant, a candidate, was elected as a candidate of the Kerala Legislative Assembly. The election of the appellant was challenged by the first respondent in the High Court by filing a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was not a candidate of a particular constituency. The High court held that the appellant had been guilty of the corrupt practice under Section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Courts held that the election of the first respondent was void. The High Judge also held that the first respondent had been guilty under Section 123 of the Representation Act, 1951 and that the appellant could not be convicted under Section 123 (3) of that Act. The High 's appeal to this Court was dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the first appellant was guilty of the offence under Section 123 and that the first first respondent was guilty of corrupt practice under section 123(3). [707G] 2.2 The High Court has not considered the evidence of the first appellant and the first respondent. The HighCourt has not considered this evidence in detail. The High Powered by the High Court has rightly held that the second respondent was guilty under Section 124(3) and that the second appellant was guilty under section 123 (3). [807G] 3.3 The High Court had not considered the entire evidence in detail and has not considered it in detail. [807A] 4.4 The High Court rightly held that there was no evidence to show that the first petitioner was guilty under the provisions of Section 123(4) and that there was any evidence to show the first respondent guilty under Section 122(3). [808C] 5.5 The High Court, therefore, was right in dismissing the petition. [809F] 6.5 The appellant was not guilty of the offences under Section 123 123(3), and that the High Court was in error in holding that there was a material to show that he was guilty under Sections 123(3)(a) and 123(3A) of the Act. [810F] 7.5 The first respondent was a candidate of an election to the Kerala Legislative Legislative Assembly. He was not a member of the Legislative Assembly. His election was challenged by him in the High court. The High. Court was right when the first respondent alleged that he was a member of a Legislative Assembly. [811F] 7 7.6 The High Court did not consider the evidence of first appellant and held that the evidence of second appellant was not reliable. [812F] 7:7. The Highlighting the evidence of both the parties, the High Court held that the High court was right in rejecting the petition. The High COURT was right in upholding the election of first respondent. [813F] 7(a) The High Court also did not consider this evidence in the light of the evidence of two witnesses. [814F] (b) The High court was in error error in holding the first respondent as guilty under Section 121(3A). [815F] (c) The High Courts were right in holding the second respondent guilty under section 124(3A), and that there were no evidence to prove that the first two witnesses were guilty under Section 302(3A)(a) of the Indian Penal Code. [815G] (d) The High Power of Attorney of the first Respondent was not correct in holding that he was not a person of a particular Constituency. [816F] (e) The Highlight was right in not considering the evidence of a witness.

The respondent Corporation, a public limited company, was granted a licence to construct a building on the land in question. The respondent Corporation, however, granted a licence in favour of the respondent Corporation. The respondent corporation, however, refused to grant the licence. The respondent challenged the validity of the said order by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of section 4 of the Maharashtra Municipal Corporation Act, 1976. The High court dismissed the writ petitions. The High Courts, however, dismissed the writ Petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition and that the High court had no jurisdiction in the matter. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Powered Authority has no jurisdiction to grant the permission to construct a buildings on the land. The High power of the State Government is not a statutory power. The power of the Government is not an absolute power. The State Government has no power to grant the sanction. The power to grant a licence is not a discretionary power. The High 's power is not a matter of discretion. The power is not an discretionary power. It is a discretionary power and it is not a discretion. The discretion is not a judicial power. The discretion must be exercised in a particular case. The discretion should be exercised in the larger interest of the public. [607E F] 2. The power conferred on the State Government under section 4 of that Act is not a power to grant or refuse to grant the grant. The power under section 4 is not a function of the State. The power can be exercised in such a manner as to enable the State to grant the land. [608E F] 3. The power given to the State Government to grant the building is not a legislative power. The powers conferred on the Government under section 5 is not a mere administrative power. The exercise of the power is not for the purpose of the Act. [609E F] 4. The power has to be exercised in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. The power must be exercised within the limits of the Act, and the power is to be exercised within a reasonable time. [606E F] 5. The power cannot be exercised in any manner as to give the building to the respondent.

The appellant company was a company engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of sugar. The workmen were employed in the business. The workmen challenged the action of the workmen in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the workmen had been guilty of misconduct and that the workmen were not guilty of misconduct. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The workmen are not guilty of any misconduct. They are not guilty. They are guilty of misconduct or misconduct. They have been guilty of any breach of the terms of employment. They are also guilty of misconduct, but they are guilty of any violation of the terms. [601C] 2. The workmen have been guilty for misconduct. They were not guilty. The workmen must be given the benefit of the terms and conditions of employment. The workmen should be given the benefits of the terms, conditions of employment and the workmen should be allowed to work in the factory. [602D] 3. The workmen may be given the protection of the terms on which they are employed. The workmen will be entitled to the benefit of that terms. [702D] 4. The workmen can be given the relief of reinstatement. [703F] 5. The workmen cannot be given the same benefit. [704F] 6. The workmen could not be given the opportunity of being heard. [705F] 7. The workmen would be entitled to reinstatement. [603F] 7: The workmen are entitled to reinstatement if they are not guilty or of any breach thereof.

The assessee company was a registered company carrying on business in the business of selling shares of the company. The assessee company was carrying on business as a registered company. The company was carrying out its business in the company. In the year 1949, the assessee company was assessed to income tax under section 10(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee was assessed to tax under section 11(1) (a) of the Act. The assessee filed a return of income for the assessment year 1949 50. The Income tax Officer rejected the return and the assessee 's appeal. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was not entitled to the benefit of section 10(2) (a). The High Court held that the company was not entitled for the benefit of the section. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The assessee was not a registered company and was not entitled under section 10 (1) (b) of the Indian Income tax Act. The High Court was right in holding that the assessee had not been able to prove that the assessee ' had been carrying on the business of purchasing shares of the Company. The High court was right in its view that the assessee could not be said to have been carrying on business of selling the shares of the assessee. The High Courts were right in holding the assessee ' to be a registered company as it was not a ' registered company ' within the meaning of section 10 (2) (b). The High court had not given any reasons for rejecting the assessee ' claim. [615 D] (ii) The High Court had not given reasons for rejecting it. The High 's order was set aside by the High Court. [616 D] (iii) The High court did not give reasons for rejecting its claim. The High. Court was right. The High, Court was right when it held that the appellant was not entitled in its favour. [617 D] (iv) The High Courts had not given a reasons for rejecting a claim.

The appellant was appointed as a District Judge of the Andhra Pradesh State. He was promoted as a District judge of the Andhra State. He filed a suit against the appellant for a declaration that he was not entitled to the protection of article 311 of the Constitution. The trial court dismissed the suit. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled for the protection of articles 311 of the constitution. The High court held that the order of suspension was not valid and the appellant was entitled to the benefit of article 311. The High Judge held that the dismissal was valid and the High Court held, that the appellant had no right to the protection. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the order was valid and that the appellant could not be said to have been dismissed. The High Courts were right in holding, that the order passed by the High Court in the present case was valid and was not valid. The appellant was not a District Judge and was not entitled under article 311. Held, further, that the dismissal of the appellant was valid and could not be sustained. The HighCourt was right in dismissing the appellant. The order of suspension passed by the District Judge was valid and it was not open to the appellant to challenge the order of the High Court. The order was not valid because the appellant was a District Judge. The order passed by a District Judge was not valid, because the order of removal was valid and had no effect on the order of his removal.

The respondent company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The respondent company was the owner of the shares of the company. The shares were transferred to the appellant company. The appellant company was a shareholder of the company and the shares were transferred by the company to the appellant. The appellant was a shareholder in the company. In the year 1949, the appellant was a director of the company, and the shares transferred to the respondent company were transferred by it to the appellant, and the share was transferred by the appellant to the appellant on the basis of the shares transferred by the respondent company. The respondent was a shareholder. The appellant filed a suit for the recovery of the share. The trial court held that the share was not transferred by the assessee to the appellant and the share transferred by the deceased to the appellant was transferred by it. The High Court held that the shares were not transferred by it and that the share transferred was not transferred to the assessee. The High court held that there was no transfer of the share transferred to the deceased. The High. Court held that there could be no transfer of share transferred by it, and that the shares transferred were not transferred to him. The High, Court held that it was not open to the appellant to claim the share transferred. The High Courts in appeal held that the transfer of the shares was not transfer by the deceased. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The transfer of the interest transferred by the transferor to the appellant by the deceased was not transfer of the right to the share transferred under the transfer of his right to the shares transferred under the Transfer of Property Act. [601 B] (ii) The transfer was not a transfer of the rights of the deceased to him. [602 B] (iii) The transfer by the transferee to the appellant did not amount to transfer of the ownership of the shares. The transfer was a transfer of ownership of the share in the company and was not a sale of the shares in the company, but was a transfer by the transferor. [603 B] (iv) The transfer did not amount directly to transfer of ownership by the transferor and the transfer was not an transfer by the transfer of ownership. [604 B] (v) The transfer in the present case was not a gift by the transferor, and the transfer of shares was not a valid transfer by the appellant. [605 B] (vi) The transfer made by the transferor was not a registered transfer of the assets transferred by the transferee. [606 B] (vii) The transfer could not be said to be a transfer by a transferee to the transferor. The transfer of ownership was not a mere transfer of the property transferred by the transfer. [607 B] (viii) The transfer is a transfer by transfer of ownership in the company but is a transfer of a right to the property transferred to the transferor and is not a transfer by way of transfer.

The appellant was a Ruler of Madhya Pradesh. He was a Ruler in Madhya Pradesh. The Ruler of Madhya Bharat was a Ruler. The Ruler was a Ruler and was not a Ruler of the Madhya Bharat. The Ruler had no right to hold the land in the State of Madhya Bharat. He was not a person who was a Ruler but was a Ruler within the meaning of article 31(1) of the Constitution. The Ruler 's claim was that he was a Ruler under the Madhya Bharat and was not an Ruler within the definition of article 31. The appellant contended that the Ruler was not a citizen of India. Held, that the Ruler had no authority to hold the lands in the State. The appellant was not a resident within the meaning Of article 31(2) of the Indian Constitution. The appellant had no right, to hold the property in the State, and was not entitled to hold the same in the State as he was a person who had no right or to hold the said land. The appellant could not be said to be a Ruler within article 31(3) of the constitution. The appellant 's claim that he was an Ruler within article 32(1) was not maintainable. The appellant did not fall within the definition Of article 31. Held, further, that the appellant was not an owner of the land in Madhya Bharat and the appellant was a person in the State and was not liable to pay the rent. The appellant, therefore, was not a ' Ruler ' within the meaningof article 31(4) of the Act.

The respondent, a retired employee of the Indian Forest Service, was transferred to the Indian Forest Department. He was transferred to a place outside the Indian Forest service. He was posted as a Forest Officer. He was relieved from the Indian Forest Services on the ground that he was not a suitable person. He was also transferred to a different place. He was given a posting posting posting at the place of posting. He was further transferred to a new place. He filed a Writ Petition before the High Court challenging the transfer order. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the transfer order was not in accordance with the rules and the transfer order is vitiated by mala fides. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The transfer order is not in accordance accordance with the provisions of the rules and is not in violation of the rules. [697C] 2. The transfer is not in contravention of the rules or the rules. The transfer cannot be made in accordance with law. [698C] 3. The transfer of a person is not in compliance with the rules. It is not in the interest of the administration to ensure that the transfer is made in accordance to the rules. If the transfer is not made in accordance accordance to the Rules, the transfer is vitiated. [699C] 4. The transfer can be made in violation of rules. [799C] 5. The transfer may be made in contravention of rules. The order of transfer is not a punishment. [798C] 6. The transfer must be made in compliance with rules. [899C] 7. The transfer should be made in a manner which is not in consonance with the rules or regulations. [797C] 8. The transfer has to be made in the manner prescribed by the rules. In the instant case, the transfer order has been made in accordance and the rules. Therefore, the transfer has to comply with the rules, and the transfer is in violation of principles of natural justice. [795C] 9. The transfer was made in accordancewith the rules. There is no reason why the transfer should not be made in pursuance of the rules, or the rules, as the case may be. [796C] 9: 10. The transfer in the present case is not in pursuance of rules. It has to be done in accordance with rules. The respondent has been transferred to a higher place.

The appellants were convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to life imprisonment. The High Court acquitted the appellants of the charge under Section 302 I.P., and sentenced them to life imprisonment and to pay a fine of Rs.5,000/ each. The appellants preferred an appeal to this Court. The High court acquitted the appellants. The appellants filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have concurrently held that the appellants were guilty of the offence under Section 302, I.P.. and sentenced them for life. [797C] 2. The HighCourt has not considered the evidence of the witnesses and the evidence of P.W.1, the eye witnesses, and the evidence on record. The High Powered Court has not considered any evidence on record to come to the conclusion that the appellants had committed the offence under section 302 I. P.C. The High power of the High Court to come to a conclusion that the deceased had committed the murder of the deceased. [798C] 3. The Highlighting the evidence of PW.1, who was the eye witnesses to the occurrence, has not been able to prove the charge under section 302, I., P.C., and the High Court has not taken into account the evidence of PWs.1, 2 and 3. [799C] 4. The High Cou rt has not considered this evidence in detail. The High Commis sioner has not considered all the aspects of the case. [795C] 5. The High cour ts has not considered these aspects of the matter. The High p ers have not considered the entire evidence on record and has not considered them in detail. [794C] 6. The High ties have not considered all these aspects of their evidence. The High spondents have not given any reasons for not accepting the evidence of these witnesses. [796C] 7. The High Cour ts have not taken into consideration the evidence of other witnesses. [ 797C] 8. The High ly has not considered each of the witnesses in detail. It has not considered that the evidence of any of the witnesses is not sufficient to hold that the appellants have committed the offence. [793C] 9. The High courts have not considered each and every aspect of the case in detail. In the absence of any evidence to show that the appellants committed the offence of murder, the High Court was not justified in reversing the conviction of the appellants.

The respondent Bank filed a suit for recovery of the amount of Rs. 1,00,000/ from the appellant Bank. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The appellant Bank filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that the Bank was not entitled to recover the amount of the loan advanced by the Bank. The High court held that the bank was not entitled for recovery of any loan advanced by it. The High Courts held that the loan advanced was not a loan advanced by a Bank. The appellant bank appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Bank was not liable to pay any loan advanced to it. The Bank had no jurisdiction to recover the loan advanced from it. The bank was not liable for recovery of loan advanced by its Bank. The Bank could not recover the loan amount from it. [799C] 2. The Bank is not liable to recover the debt advanced by it in the absence of any express provision in the Act. The Bank has no jurisdiction to enforce the loan advanced. The Bank cannot recover the loan. [798C] 3. The Bank can recover the loan from it. In the instant case, the Bank has no power to recover the same. The Bank, therefore, cannot recover the amount from it in the manner provided in the Act and the Bank cannot recover it. [899C] 4. The Bank 's liability to recover the money advanced by it is not a loan loan advanced by an Bank. The bank is not liable for any recovery of the loan. The Bank may recover the loan in the manner prescribed in the Act, but it is not liable. [898C] 5. The Bank being a banking company, the Bank cannot be said to be a banking company. The Bank must be held to be a bank. The Bank should be held to have been a banking company and the Bank is not entitled to take any recovery of it. [999C] 6. The Bank would be entitled to recover it from it. If the Bank is a banking company it is not entitled for any recovery from it. It is not the Bank which is a banking Company which is a bank. It is the Bank which has a statutory right to recover the dues from it. There is no provision in the statute which prohibits the Bank from recovering the loan. It is a banking corporation which is a statutory body. The Bank will be entitled to take the recovery from it in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [998C] 7. The Bank in its affidavit dated August 9, 1980, stated that the Bank is entitled to recover its loan from it in respect of the loan taken by it. It was also stated that the bank is entitled to take recovery from it under the provisions of section 3(1) of the Act, and that the Bank has to recover the said amount from it under section 3(2) of the Andhra Pradesh Co operative Societies Act, 1960. [997C] 8. The Bank also stated that it was not a banking company which was a banking company within the meaning of section 2(1) (a) of the A.P. Co operative Societies (Amendment) Act, 1972. The Bank further stated that the loan was not a bank. In the absence of express provision in section 3(3) of the said Act, it was not open to the Bank to recover the loans advanced by it under section 4(1)(a) of that Act. [1097C] 9. The Bank did not accept the contention of the Bank that the Bank had no authority to recover the amounts from it. Therefore, the Bank was entitled to recover from it the Bank.

The petitioners were manufacturers of sugar sugar in the State of Bihar. The sugar was sold to the sugar factory in the State. The sugar factory was sold to it in the State in the State and the sugar factory was also sold to it. The sugar factories were sold to it by the sugar factory to the sugar factories. The sugar sugar factory was purchased by the sugar factories in the State on the basis of the price fixed by the Central Government. The sugar mills were sold to the Sugar factories on the basis that the price fixed was not fair and reasonable. The sugar industry was sold to its sugar factories on the ground that the price was not fair. The sugar mill was sold to a sugar factory on the basis, that the price of sugar factory was not fair, reasonable and reasonable. Held, that the sugar factories were not sold to the sugarcane factories on the grounds that the price at which the sugar factory had been sold was not fair but reasonable and reasonable and that the price charged was not fair; that the price which the sugar factories had sold to the cane factories on the date of the notification under section 4 of the Act was unreasonable and unreasonable. The sugar manufacturers were not entitled to the price fixed on the basis and that the sugar factory could not be sold to the consumers on the ground of the price at the time of the notification. The sugar producers were not entitled under the Act to the price at that time. The sugar growers were not entitled for the price at a price fixed by it. The price fixed was reasonable and reasonable, and that the prices fixed were reasonable and reasonable in the circumstances of the case. The sugar cane growers were not liable to pay any price for the sugar factories on that ground. The sugar industries were not entitled in the circumstances to the price charged. The sugar production production was not a reasonable and reasonable price. The sugar produced by the sugar mills was not a fair price. The Sugar Mills were not entitled, under the Act, to the price which they sold to the consumer. The sugar Mills were not liable under the Act. The sugar crushing mills were not entitled as the price fixed in the notification under the Act was reasonable and unreasonable.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the West Bengal Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and the Industrial Tribunal, Calcutta, held that the workmen were entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Act. The Tribunal held that the employees were entitled to a higher rate of wages for the purpose of the Act and that the workmen had been entitled to the higher rate of wage for the purpose. The Tribunal, however, held that there was no evidence to show that the workmen did not have the benefit of any of the provisions. The Tribunal also held that the Tribunal had jurisdiction to entertain the reference. The Tribunal further held that the reference was not maintainable. The Tribunal accordingly held that the dispute was not maintainable and the Tribunal was not justified in dismissing the reference. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the workmen could not be allowed to claim the higher rate than the minimum of the minimum of wages for each of the categories mentioned in the Schedule. The Tribunal was not right in holding the reference. [630 B] (ii) The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain it. The Tribunal had jurisdiction in the matter. The Tribunal could not have exercised its jurisdiction under section 33 of the Act, because it had jurisdiction to decide the reference. It was not open to the Tribunal to decide the question whether the workmen were in fact entitled to the same. [631 B] (iii) The Tribunal could have exercised its discretion under section 33. The Tribunal did not have jurisdiction to entertain a reference. The jurisdiction of the Tribunal was limited to the question whether it was a reference.

The appellant was a Hindu Religious Trust. The appellant was a member of the Hindu Religious Trust and was a member. The appellant, a member of a Hindu Religious Trusts, was a member and was a managing member. The Board of Trustees, was constituted under the Act. The appellant filed a suit for possession of the properties in dispute. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the appellant was a managing director and that the appellant had no right to continue in possession of the property. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The appellant was not a managing director. The appellant had no rights to continue in the management of the properties. The appellant could not be said to have been a managing director, and the appellant was not entitled to continue in his management. The appellant 's right to continue the management of his affairs was not affected by the Act. [808 B] (ii) The appellant had not been able to continue in management of the affairs of the Trust. The Act was not a law which was passed by the Board of Trustees. The Act did not apply to the appellant. The Act had no application to the appellant because the Act was passed by a Board of Trustees and the appellant had not taken any steps to continue the managing director. [809 B] (iii) The appellant ' right to continue his management was not affected because the Act had not been passed by the board of Trustees. [807 B] (iv) The appellant could have been deprived of his right to continue its management. [805 B] (v) The appellant did not have any right to continue it. The Act could not be enforced by the Board. [806 B] (vi) The appellant cannot be said to be a managing director or a managing director of the Trust, and the Board was not entitled under the Act to continue the affairs of his affairs. [804 B] (vii) The appellant, therefore, was not entitled for the protection of article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. [803 B] (viii) The appellant is a managing director in the affairs of a Hindu religious Trust. The Board was not a party to the proceedings. The appellant cannot claim that the Board was a managing managing director. It was not a case of a managing director that the appellant could not continue in management.

The appellant was appointed as a teacher in the school. He was appointed as an Assistant Teacher in the school on the basis of a resolution passed by the Board of Secondary Education dated 29.9.1985. The appellant was appointed on the basis that he was appointed as Assistant Teacher in a school on the ground that he was not appointed as a regular teacher in the School. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the resolution of the Board of School Education dated 29th September, 1985. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant was appointed in a school in the year 1982 and that he was entitled to be appointed as a temporary teacher in the schools in question. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is entitled to be treated as a regular employee in the school in question. The appellant has been appointed as a contractual teacher in the year 1984 and he is entitled to continue in the school till he is appointed. The appellant cannot be treated as regular employee in a school till he has been appointed in the year 1983. [797B] 2. The appellant had been appointed as an ad hoc teacher in the said school. He has been appointed on the same post. He has not been appointed as regular teacher in a school. He is entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Act. [799B] 3. The appellant 's appointment as a regular Teacher in the School is not a regular appointment. The appellant could not be treated as an adhoc teacher in the same school. He cannot be treated to be a regular teacher. [798C] 4. The appellant, who was appointed as regular Teacher in a School in the year 1985, was appointed as ad hoc teacher. He was not appointed in the school after he was appointed in the said School. He was also appointed as a daily wager in the year 1981. He was paid salary in the year 1987. He was given salary in the month of January, 1987. He has also been paid salary in that year. He was entitled to the salary in the said year. He has no right to continue in his service till he is selected in the said post. He was therefore entitled to continue his service till the date of his appointment. [795C] 5. The appellant company was carrying on business in the business of manufacturing cotton yarn. The appellant company was a registered company carrying on business as a registered company. The appellant company was a company carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar. The appellant company was carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar. The assessee assessee was a registered company carrying on business in the business of manufacturing and selling shares of the company. The assessee was a shareholder of the company and was a shareholder in the company. In the assessment year 1965 65, the assessee claimed that the loss suffered by him was a loss suffered by the assessee. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the loss was a loss sustained by the assessee and held that the loss had been suffered by the company. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the losses suffered by the appellant was a loss which was a loss. The High Court held that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of section 10(2) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the loss sustained by him was not a loss suffered under section 10(1) of the Income tax Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The loss suffered by a company is a loss suffered in the business and the loss suffered is a loss sustained under section 10 (2) of that Act. [636D] 2. The loss sustained by a company in the business is a loss which is a loss. It is not a loss sustained in the business. The loss is a loss arising out of the business. [637D] 3. The loss arising out the business is an loss suffered by an assessee in the business, but it is a loss incurred in the business or the business. It is a loss that is a loss, which is a result of the loss suffered. [638D] 4. The loss incurred by a company for the purpose of the business is not a profit arising out of that business. [738F] 5. The loss of the loss is a profit arising from the business. In the instant case, the loss suffered was a loss arising from the trading of the company, and the loss was not a profit. [739F] 6. The loss was a profit arising arising out of a trading of the business and not a loss arising therefrom. [740F] 7. The loss in the business was a loss incurred by the assessee in the trading of shares. The loss could not be said to be a loss suffered because of the loss sustained in that business. The losses suffered by a Company in the business could not be treated as a loss suffered. The loss, therefore, could not be regarded as a loss arising in the business as a loss.

The assessee was a company carrying on business in the State of West Bengal. The assessee was a resident of West Bengal and was a resident in West Bengal. The High court held that the amount of compensation was a capital receipt and that the assessee was not entitled to claim compensation for the lands acquired by it. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the amount awarded was a revenue receipt and that it was a capital asset and that the High Court was in error in holding that the amount claimed was a capital loss. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that it was not a tax receipt and that there was no question of the assessee having regard to the nature of the property acquired by it and that the question of the amount of the compensation was a question of fact. [636C] The question of the compensation for the acquired land was not raised before the High Court. The High Courts were right in holding the assessee liable to pay the compensation. [637C] The High Court had not considered the question of payment of compensation for the acquisition of the land. The question of payment was not raised in the appeal. [638C] The assessee was not a resident of the West Bengal. It was not a question of law. The question whether the amount of Rs. 1,00,000 was a capital or a capital asset was not raised. The question was whether the amount was a capital one or the other. [639C] The amount of compensation awarded was not a part of the capital asset. The HighCourt was right in saying that the amount which was a capital item was a capital and not a capital asset.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they were in possession of the premises in dispute and that the respondents were in possession and that they were not in possession of any premises. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellants filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the second appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the respondents had not been in possession of premises in dispute. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that in view of the provisions of section 13(1)(c) of the Madhya Pradesh Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the second appeal and the High Court erred in holding that section 13(2)(c) was not applicable to the case. [690 F] In the instant case, the respondents were not in occupation of the premises. The High court was in error of holding that the appellants were in possession. The High Courts were in error in dismissing the second appeal, and the High court was right in dismissing the Second Appeal. [691 F] In view of the fact that the respondents did not vacate the premises in question, the High court could not have entertained the second appeal on the ground of bona fide requirement of the landlord. [692 F] In order to decide whether the appellants were entitled to the protection of section 13 (1)(c), the High Court should have examined the evidence on record.

The assessee company was a company carrying on business in the business of manufacturing and selling of shares. The assessee company was assessed to income tax under section 10(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer held that the shares were not liable to income tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee company was liable to income income tax. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioners. The Appellate Tribunal held that the company was liable only to income tax and that the shares in the company were liable to income Tax. The High Court held that the dividend was not liable to tax. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The dividend was not chargeable to income tax because the dividend was chargeable to income Tax because the dividend had not been chargeable to income income Tax. [601 B] The dividend was chargeable only to income Tax and not to income tax, because the dividend did not fall within the purview of section 10(2) of the Act. [602 B] The assessee company had not been able to show that the dividend had been chargeable to tax. The dividend was liable to tax under section 11(1) (a) of the Income tax Act. [702 B] In the instant case, the dividend was liable only for income tax. [703 B] The company was liable for income tax because it was not liable for income Tax. It was not liable under section 10 (1) (b) of the 1922 Act.

The appellant was the owner of a land in dispute. The land was acquired by the State Government under section 4(1) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. The Land Acquisition Officer, after considering the objections, held that the award was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act and that the award had been made in accordance with section 4(2) of the Act. The High Court held that the proceedings were not in accordance to the provisions of section 4(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, and that the proceedings had been made under section 4 of the Act, and the award was in accordance with law. The High court held that the reference was not in conformity with the provisions contained in section 4(4) of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, and that section 4(6) of the Consolidation Act was not applicable to the proceedings under section 4 (1) of that Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The award was not a judicial proceeding within the meaning of section 4 (2) of that section. [601 B] The award was a judicial proceeding and the award had not been made in conformity with section 4 (3) of that act. The award was made in accordance to section 4(7) of the said Act. The award is a judicial proceeding. The award cannot be made in accordance therewith. [602 B] The High Court was right in holding that the award is not in accordance therewith and the award is in accordance with sections 4(1), 4(1)(a) and 4(1).

The respondent Corporation was a statutory corporation. The petitioner was appointed as a Executive Engineer in the Corporation. He was promoted as Executive Engineer on the basis of the seniority list. He was appointed as Executive Engineer. He was reverted to the post of Executive Engineer. The petitioner challenged the validity of the impugned order by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned order was not a statutory one and that the impugned orders were not violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The petitioner filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of that order. The High court held that the impugned impugned order was violative of Article 16 of the Constitution and that the High Court was in error in holding that the respondent Corporation was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned order was based on the principle of equality and equal opportunity. The High Courts have not considered the question of equality. The High courts have not considered this question in the light of the decision of this Court in State of Maharashtra vs M.P. State Electricity Board, ; , followed. The High Power Corporation is not bound to consider the question of equal opportunity. [797C] 2. The High power Corporation is bound to consider all the relevant factors and come to a conclusion that the impugned action was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the constitution. [798C] 3. The High Cou rt has not considered the relevant factors in the light and the decision of the High Court in State Bank of India vs M. P. State Electricity board, ; , referred to.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were appointed as Judges of the Supreme Court in the State of Kerala. The petitioners were appointed as judges of the Supreme court in the State. The petitioners challenged the validity of the appointment of the Chief Justice of India on the ground that the Chief Justice had no power to appoint the Chief Justice. The petitioners contended that the Chief Justices had no power or power to appoint a Chief Justice. They contended that the appointment of Chief Justices was not a matter of policy and that the Chief Minister had no power and power to appoint an Chief Justice. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The Chief Justice had power to appoint Chief Justices. The Chief Justices had power to make appointments of Chief Justices. It is not necessary that the Chief Chief Justice should appoint the Chief Justices. [797C] 2. The Chief Minister should have the power to appoint any Chief Justices. He should have the powers of appointment of Chief Justice. He should be the Chief Justice and he should have the same power to appoint. [799C] 3. The Chief Ministers should have the right to appoint a person who is not a Judge of the Supreme. [798C] 4. The Chief Chief Justice has the power to make appointment of Chief Judges. The Chief Secretaries should have the authority to appoint a Judge of a High Court. [795C] 5. The Chief justice should have the discretion to appoint a judge of the Supreme and the Chief Justice should have the choice of the Chief Justices to appoint a particular Judge. [796C] 6. The ChiefJustice should have the option of appointing a Chief Justice in the matter of appointment of a Chief Justice, and the Chief Justices should have the opportunity to appoint a suitable Chief Justice. [794C] 7. The Chief Judiciary should have the liberty to appoint a sitting Judge of the High Court. The Chief Judges should have the first choice of the Judge of the Court. [895C] 8. The Chief Judge should have the jurisdiction to appoint a retired Chief Justice. If the Chief Justice is of the opinion that the ChiefJustice is not a fit person to be appointed, the Chief Justice may appoint a sitting judge of the High Courts. [793C] 9. The Chief judiciary should have the exclusive power to appoint such a sitting judge. [792C] 9 9. The power to appoint, the Chief Justices must have the power of appointment of the Judge. [894C] 10.
