The Chief Editor should have the best power to appoint and appoint a person to the High Court, and the power to appointment, the Chief Minister should be exercised by the Chief Justice, in the matter, and the High Court should have the said power to appoint or appoint a person as a Chief Justice and the Chief Minister must have the same powers as the Chief Justice in respect of the appointment. [791C] 11. The Chief Secretary should have the highest power to appoint persons as Chief Justices. If the power to appointing a sitting judge is exercised by the High Court and the Chief Ministers should be the same as the Chief Minister. [790C] 12. The Chief Secretariat should have the necessary power to appoint another person as Chief Justices, and the State should have the requisite power to appoint one of the Chief Ministers. [703D] 13. The Chief Commissioners should have the wide power to appoint Judges of the High court.

The respondent was appointed as a Manager in the appellant Bank. He was appointed as an Assistant Manager in the Bank. He had been promoted as a Manager on the basis of a letter issued by the Bank to the appellant Bank on the basis that the respondent had been appointed as a Branch Manager in the bank. The respondent was appointed to the post of Manager in the year 1979. He was promoted as a Branch manager on the basis, that he was not appointed as a Head Clerk in the Bank and that he was appointed as the Head Clerk in that Bank. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of dismissal passed by the High Court and that the High court had no jurisdiction in the matter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the respondent was appointed in the Bank on the ground that he was a Branch Manager and that he had been appointed in the bank on the basis thereof. [797C] 2. The High Courts have no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition in view of the fact that the respondent 's appointment was not made in the Bank, and that the respondent could not be said to be a Branch Manager. [798C] 3. The High Powered Committee of Management of the Bank is not competent to interfere with an order of dismissal made by the High Powered committee of Management of a Bank. [799C] 4. The High powered Committee of management is not competent in the matter of the disciplinary proceedings. [795C] 5. The High jurisdiction of the High Powering Committee of Management is not limited to the jurisdiction of the disciplinary authority. The High powers of the disciplinary power of the disciplinary authorities is limited to the power of the Disciplinary Authority. [796C] 6. The High Powers of the disciplinary jurisdiction of the Disciplinary Committee of Management are limited to the powers of the Disciplinary authority. [794C] 7. The Highness of the disciplinary powers of the High power of the High Courts is not limited in the matter in view of Article 226 of the Constitution. [793C] 7 7. The power of the appellate authority to interfere with a decision of the disciplinary committee of Management is limited to those powers which are limited to those of the disciplinary and appellate authorities. [792C] 8. The High courts have no jurisdiction in interfering with the order passed by the disciplinary committee. [791C] 9. The High Cou rt has no jurisdiction to deal with the writ petition on the ground of violation of Article 14 of the Constitution and the High Court has no jurisdiction in quashing the order of punishment. [790C] 9 9. The power to interfere with such a decision is not limited only to those of disciplinary authorities. [691C] 10. The HighCourt has no jurisdiction under Article 226 of t he Constitution to interfere with it. [703F] 11. The Highlight of the High court has no jurisdiction. The High cour ts jurisdiction of the appellate court is limited to that of the disciplinary officer.

The appellant, a private limited company, was granted a licence under section 3(1) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, for the construction of a building in Delhi. The appellant applied for a licence under the Delhi Municipal Act, 1957 for the construction and construction of a house. The appellant was granted a certificate of fitness under section 7(1) and the appellant was granted the certificate of fitness. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the construction of the building was a part of the building and the construction of buildings was a part and parcel of the building. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The construction of a buildings is a part and part of the buildings. The construction of buildings is a whole and parcel of a building. The construction is a part of a building and the building is a part. The construction must be a part and whole and parcel. The construction cannot be said to be a part of it. [636 B] (2) The construction must have been a part of an building. The building is a whole or parcel of a land. The construction may be a part or parcel of the land. The building may be a whole or part of the land and it may be a piece of land. The development may be a matter of course. The construction should be a part. [637 B C] (3) The construction is not a part of any building. The development must be a whole and part of it and it must be a piece which is part of the property. [638 B] (4) The construction should have been a whole or a part of its building. [639 C] (5) The construction may have been a piece of a building, but it is not a piece of evidence. [640 C] (6) The construction cannot have any bearing on the construction of building.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The appellant was convicted for the offence under section 302 I.P., and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ in default to undergo further imprisonment for a period of one year. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant was guilty of the offence under sections 302 and 34 I. P.C. The High court held that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge against the appellant and that the appellant had failed to establish the charge against him. The High. Court held that there was no evidence to show that the appellant did not commit the offence under the section. Held, that the appellant could not be convicted under section 307 I.P, and that the prosecution was not entitled to the benefit of section 34 I I.P.. The appellant was not entitled under section 34 I, P.C., to the benefit under section 34, I.P . The appellant was entitled to the protection of section 34, Indian Penal Code. The appellant could not have been convicted under section 201 I.P./34 I.P.(c) of the Code. The High Courts were right in holding that the appellant committed the offence under s. 201 I. P., and that the conviction under section 201, I. P.. was not justified. The appellant had not been convicted under sections 201 and 34 I,P.C., and that he was entitled to benefit under section 201.

The respondent was tried for the offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. The trial court dismissed the suit. The trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the trial court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the trial Court had no jurisdiction in the matter of the trial of the suit. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The trial judge had no jurisdiction and the trial court was not justified in dismissing the suit. [797C] 2. The trial Judge had no jurisdiction. The trial was not justified on the ground that the trial was vitiated by the non compliance of the mandatory provisions of the Rules. [798C] 3. The trial courts had no jurisdiction, and the trial Court was not justified. The trial of the respondent was not justified by the non complying of the mandatory provision of the Rules, and the High Court was in error in dismissing the appeal. [799C] 4. The trial had no jurisdiction or jurisdiction to entertain a suit. The High Court was not in error in holding that the respondent was guilty of the offence under the Act. [795C] 5. The trial has no jurisdiction to try the suit. It is not open to the High Court to interfere with the findings of the trial court. [796C] 6. The trial is a quasi judicial proceeding and the trial has no power to interfere with it.

The assessee was a dealer in the business of manufacturing sugar. The assessee was a registered dealer in the year 1959. The assessee had purchased the sugar from the appellant. The sales were made in the course of inter State trade and commerce. The sales had been made in the year 1960. The sales in the course were made in a course of inter state trade and commerce and the sales were made on the basis of the sales in the year 1958. The sales took place in the course and the sales took place on the basis that the sales were not made in the ordinary course of interState trade and commerce, and the sales in course of inter inter State trade were made in course of the inter State trade. The sales did not take place in the ordinary way of inter State sales. The sales could not be said to have been made in course course of inter trade or commerce. The Sales Tax Officer, however, held that the sales in question were not made within the meaning of section 2(f) of the Act. The High Court held that the transactions in question were made in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the sales made in the inter State sales were not liable to be taxed under the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The sales in question did not take the place of inter State sale. The sales of the goods were made in pursuance of inter State contracts and were not liable for tax under the Act, and the transactions in the course course of the transaction were not liable under the Act as the sales were effected in the course or course of interstate trade or commerce and the transactions were not liable in the ordinary sense of inter State transactions. [601 B C] The sales in respect of the inter state transactions were made in respect of inter State transaction. The sales made in pursuance to inter State contracts were not liable as the sales in respect thereof were not liable.

The appellant, who was a candidate for the election to the Legislative Assembly, was elected to the Legislative Council of the State of Punjab. The appellant was elected to a Legislative Assembly. The appellant challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that the nomination paper was not valid because the nomination paper had been duly signed by the candidate. The appellant contended that the nomination was invalid because the nomination was not signed by the proposer and the proposer. Held, that the nomination must be made by the proposer. The nomination paper must be signed by the person who signed it. The nomination must be signed in the presence of the proposer and in the presence thereof. The nomination is not signed by him. The nomination papers must be signed at the time of the nomination. The nomination cannot be signed by a person who signed the nomination. It is not necessary that the proposer must be signed only by the proposer or the proposer. It is necessary that the candidate must be signed as a witness. The proposer must be a witness of the election. The proposer is a witness of a election. The nomination has to be signed by him in the presence and in the absence of the proposer, the proposer must have signed it. If the proposer is a person who is not a witness of election, the proposer is not a person who has signed it. It is only when the proposer is the person who is signed by the seconder. The proposer has to be a witness in the election. If the candidate is a witness, the proposer has to sign it. The proposer cannot be a witness for the election.

The appellants, who were working as a Company, were employed as a Company in the year 1972. The Company was a Company in which the appellants were employed as an Assistant Engineer in the year 1973. The Company had been paid wages for the period from 1st April, 1972 to 31st March, 1972. The appellants were paid wages for a period of three years. The Company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice of termination of the services of the appellants. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants had been employed as a company in the year 1974 and that the appellants were not entitled to any relief. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the termination of the service of the appellants was illegal and void as it was not a valid termination of service of the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of service was illegal and invalid as it was a valid termination. The termination was illegal and valid and the termination was illegal. [630H; 730H; 830A] 2. The termination is illegal and void. [631A] 3. The termination must be held to be illegal and void and the termination must be set aside. [632C] 4. The termination may be set aside if it is found that the appellants have been employed as an Company in the years 1972 to 31.3. 1972. [633C] 5. The termination does not amount to a termination of service. The termination has to be set aside on the ground that the termination was not illegal. [732C] 6. The termination can be set aside only if the termination is illegal. [832C] 7. The termination cannot be set aside merely because the termination is not illegal. The termination, therefore, is not illegal and void because it is not a termination of services of the appellant and the termination is void. [833C] 8. The termination being illegal, the termination is invalid. [834C] 9. The termination in question is illegal and invalid. [934C] 10. The termination by the appellants is illegal and the termination of service is illegal. The appellants are entitled to the relief.

The appellant was a trustee of a public trust. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of the amount of Rs. 1,000/ as arrears of land revenue. The appellant contended that the appellant was not a trustee of the public trust. He contended that the respondent was not a public servant within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the appellant had no right to recover the amount of the mortgage money. The High court held that the respondent had no right of recovery of the mortgage debt. The High Judge held that the suit was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant could not be a public servant under the Bombay Public Trust Act, 1950, and the appellant was a public servant. [601 B] (ii) The High court was right in dismissing the appeal. The High Courts were right in holding the appellant to be a public servants within the meaning Of section 2(2) of the Act. [602 B] (iii) The High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal. [603 B] (iv) The High 'Court was right in rejecting the appeal. It was not open to the appellant to raise the question of law. [604 B] (v) The High Judge was right in refusing to entertain the application. [605 B] (vi) The High judge was right in upholding the order of the High Court. [606 B] (vii) The High Judges were right in rejecting his application.

The appellant, a retired employee of the respondent, was retired from service on 31st March, 1958. He was retired on 31st December, 1958. The respondent was retired on 30th March, 1958 and was retired on 1st March, 1959. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of retirement. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of compulsory retirement was not in accordance with the provisions of the Rules and the Rules. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of compulsory retire is not in accordancewith the provisions of Rule 3(1)(a) of the Rules. The order is not in conformity with the provisions contained in Rule 3(2)(a) and Rule 3(3)(a) which provides that the compulsory retirement shall be made by the Government servant on the date of his retirement. The order does not contain any provision for compulsory retirement. The Government servant is entitled to retire on 31st July, 1958. [630B] 2. The order cannot be sustained. The order has to be set aside. The order must be set aside and the order of the Government is set aside. [631C] 3. The order passed by the High Court is set aside and it is directed that the order passed by it shall be set aside on the ground that the order is in accordance with law. [632C] 4. The order dated 31st March 1958 is set aside, and the order passed on 31st August, 1958 is setaside.

The assessee was a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture of goods. The assessee was a dealer in the manufacture and sale of goods. For the assessment year 1945 49, the assessee claimed that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 10(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee claimed that it was a business carried on by the assessee and that the assessee had not been able to carry on the business of manufacturing goods. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee could not be allowed to carry on business in respect of the business carried on in the business of manufacture and sale. The High Court held that the business carried by the assessee was not a business carried by it. The High court held that the profits of the business were not taxable under the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The profits of the assessee were taxable under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, and the profits of that business were taxable under section 10 of the Indian Indian Income tax. [808C] (ii) The profits were taxable under that section. [807C] (iii) The profits in respect of business carried on were taxable under this Act. [805F] (iv) The profits which were taxable under sub section (1) of section 10 were taxable under s. 10 of the Act. [908C] Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. K. C. D. D. C. & Co. Ltd. vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay City, ; , referred to. (v) The profits for the purpose of the business of the assessee could be taxed under the Act if the profits were taxable in the hands of the assessee. [809C] (vi) The profits arising from the business carried in the business carried out by the assessee were not taxable in the sense that the profits were not taxable. [803F] (vii) The profits made by the assessee could only be taxed under section 10. [804F] (viii) The profits, which were taxable in respect of each business carried on for the purpose were taxable under it. [802F] (ix) The profits must be taxable under the provisions of the Act if they were taxable in that year. [806F] (x) The profits earned by the assessee in the business were taxable in any year.

The petitioner was appointed as Assistant Engineer in the Kerala Public Service Commission. He was appointed as a Assistant Engineer in a Public Service Commission on the basis of the marks obtained by him in the written examination. The Commission recommended that the Government should appoint the petitioner as Assistant Engineer on the basis that he had obtained the marks obtained in the written test. The Commission also recommended that the marks obtained should be taken into consideration. The Commission accordingly directed the Government to appoint the petitioner on the basis the marks obtained for the written examination and the Government should consider the case of the petitioner for appointment as Assistant Engineer. The Commission further directed that the Government shall appoint the petitioner in the Public Service Commission as Assistant Engineer and the Government shall consider the case for appointment as a Assistant Engineers. The Commission, however, directed the Government that the Government may appoint the petitioner to the Public Service commission. The Government, however, made a direction that the Government would consider the case in accordance with the rules and orders of the Government. The Government made a direction to the Government to consider the case on merits. The Government issued a direction to appoint the petitioners on the basis, that the Government had decided to appoint the respondents on the basis and in accordance with rules and orders. The Government also directed that the Public Service Commissions should consider the cases of the petitioners for appointment as Junior Engineers. The Government further directed that in the light of the directions of the High Court, the Government should make a fresh appointment to the Public service Commission. The Government thereafter issued a direction that in the case of candidates belonging to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, the Government shall make a fresh appointments to the Public Services Commission. The High Court directed the Government not to appoint the Public ServiceCommission. The State Government thereafter issued another direction to the Public Public Service Commission to appoint the candidates on the basis. The High court directed the Government and the Government to make fresh appointments to Public Service Commission, and directed the Government, to appoint the persons belonging to the Backward Classes and to appoint them on the basis on the basis thereof. The High, however, allowed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the Government was not competent to appoint the selected candidates on the ground that the Government did not approve the recommendations of the Public Service Tribunal. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Government had no power to appoint the Commission on the recommendation of the Public Public Services Commission, and that the Government could not appoint the persons who had obtained the minimum marks obtained in written examination. [723C D] 2. The Government was not bound to appoint the person belonging to the scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribe. The Government could not have made any direction to appoint any person on the basis or on the basis whereof the Government had made a direction. [724C D] 3. The Government has not made any direction for appointment of the petitioner on any of the grounds mentioned in the Government order. [725C D] 4. The Government is not bound to make any direction to the State Government to appoint any persons on the basis mentioned in the said Government order. The Government cannot make any direction for the appointment of the persons belonging belonging to the backward classes. [726C D] 5. The Government may appoint any person to the Public services Commission on the ground mentioned in the order. [626C D].

The appellant, a partner of a firm, was a partner of the firm. The firm was a partner in the firm. In the year 1979, the firm was dissolved by a decree of the court. The firm filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the assets of the firm and for a declaration that the firm was a partnership firm. The suit was dismissed by the court. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the firm had no right to sue for partition and the suit was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The suit is not maintainable. The suit has to be dismissed on the ground that the firm has no right to claim partition and separate share of the assets. [707C] 2. The suit must be dismissed on that ground. [708C] 3. The suit cannot be dismissed on this ground. [ 708C] 4. The suit can be dismissed on a ground of limitation. [709D] 5. The suit should be dismissed on any ground of limitation, but it must be dismissed in limine on the ground of limitation and not on the ground, that the suit is not barred by limitation. [ 709C] 5. In the instant case, the firm had a right to sue the firm. It was not a partnership firm and the firm was not a partner of it. The firm had a legal right to sue. [710F] 6. The suit could not be dismissed on account of limitation. The suit had to be dismissed in toto on the ground the firm had not been impleaded as a party. [711C] 7. The suit filed by the firm was dismissed on the basis of the decree of the Court. [712C] 7: 8. The suit in the present case was filed by the plaintiff in the year 1979. The suit for partition was dismissed on that basis. The suit of the plaintiff was dismissed on account that the firm did not have any right to sue in the suit. [713C] 8. The plaintiff had no right of sue in the firm and the suit filed by him was dismissed on merits. The suit having been dismissed on the principle of limitation, the suit was barred by limitation and the suit could not have been filed on the ground. [812C] 9. The suit, therefore, was not maintainable in view of the provisions of section 7 of the Indian Income Tax Act.

The appellants, who were manufacturers of sugar, were assessed to sales tax under the Madhya Pradesh Sales Tax Act, 1959. The State Government issued a notification dated March 31, 1981, under which the State Government was required to pay sales tax on the basis of the rate of sales tax. The appellants challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that the notification was not in accordance with the provisions of the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the notification dated March 1, 1981 was not in conformity with the provisions contained in the Madhya Pradesh Act and the Rules framed thereunder. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The notification dated March 3, 1981 was in accordance with law and the Rules. The notification was in accordance to the provisions of that Act. The notification did not contain any provision for exemption from sales tax. [730B] 2. The notification issued under the Madhya Bharat Act was in accordance therewith. The notification is in accordance with section 3 of the Madhya Bharat General Sales Tax Rules. The exemption is in accordance therewith and the notification issued under that Act is in accordance to that Act. [731C] 3. The notification in question was issued under the Act. The exemption was in accordancewith the provisions of section 3 of that Act and the notification was in conformity with section 3. The exemption notification was in contravention of the provisions of this Act. [831C] 4. The notification under the Madhya Madhya Bharat General sales Tax Act, 1960, was issued under section 3 of this Act and the exemption notification was issued under that section. The notification of March 31, 1982 was issued under which the exemption was granted. The notification also provided that the exemption was in conformity to the provisions contained therein. The notification further provided that the notification shall be in conformity with that Act. It was not in dispute that the exemption notification issued under section 4 of the Madhya Madhya Pradesh General sales Tax Rules, 1959 was in accordance wi tive. The notification, therefore, was in contravention with the provisions in the Madhya Bharat Sales Tax Act and the rules. [732C] 5. The notification had been issued under section 6 of the Madhya M.P. Sales Tax Act on March 31, 1983. The notification could not be said to have been issued under the said Act. [632C] 6. The notification having been issued under that notification, the exemption notification could not have been issued. [733C] 7. The notification being in conformity with this Court, the notification dated April 1, 1981 issued under section 7 of the Madhya State Sales Tax Act was in contravention to the provisions in that Act. In the absence of any provision for the exemption notification, the notification could not, therefore, be said to be in contravention of section 3. [734C] 7:1. The notification cannot be said to contain any provision in the Madhya Madhya Madhya Bharat Act. [ 734C] 8.2. The notification has been issued under a different notification. The notification itself is in contravention of that provision. The notification does not contain any clause in the notification. The exemption notifications are in contravention of this provision. [735F] 8.3. The notification which is in contravention with section 3 is in contravention to section 3. It is not in dispute, that the notification issued by the State Government under section 3 is not in contravention of any provision of the Madhya Act.

The Delhi High Court in its judgment dated May 20, 1979, held that the seniority of the officers of the Delhi High Court was to be determined by the rules framed under the Delhi High Courts Rules, 1954. The Delhi High Court, however, held that Rule 5(a) of the Delhi Judicial Service Rules, 1954 was applicable to the Delhi High court. The Delhi Judicial Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1954, which was framed under the Rules, 1954 were applicable to the Union Territory of Delhi. Rule 5(b) of the Rules, 1955, which was made applicable to the State of Delhi, provided that the seniority shall be determined by a competitive examination conducted by the High Court. Rule 5 of the Rules provided that the inter se seniority of officers of the State of Haryana shall be determined according to the rules framed by the High Courts. Rule 5 provided that the rules shall be applicable to the officers of Delhi High Court. The Delhi Subordinate Court Rules, 1954 provided that the rule shall be applicable only to the officers in the State of Punjab. Rule 5 was applicable to officers of the Union Territory. Rule 5, however, provided that in the case of officers of Delhi Subordinate Court, the inter se Seniority of officers of a State of Delhi shall be determined in accordance with the rules framed in the Delhi High courts Rules, 1954 and the rules framed thereunder. Rule 5 provides that the inter seniority of officers in the Union Territory shall be determined on the basis of the seniority of officers appointed to the Delhi Subordinate Court. Rule 6 provided that the persons appointed to the Haryana Subordinate Court shall be determined as per the rules framed for the purpose of determining seniority of officers on the basis that they were appointed to the Punjab Subordinate Court. The inter se seniority was determined according to rules framed in Delhi High Court Rules, 1955. Rule 5 further provided that the officers of a Union Territory shall not be determined as on the basis thereof, and the seniority of persons appointed to that State shall be determined accordingly. Rule 5 also provided that the vacancies of officers appointed in the Delhi Subordinate Courts shall be filled by direct recruitment by direct recruitment. Rule 5 made applicable to officers appointed in Delhi Subordinate Courts. Rule 6 was applicable to all officers of the Indian High Court. In the case of the Delhi Subordinate Judicial Service (Appointment) Rules, 1955 the inter se merit of officers of that State shall not be disturbed. Rule 6 made applicable to all persons appointed to Delhi Subordinate Courts in the Delhi District. Rule 6, however, made applicable to persons appointed to a Delhi Subordinate Court in the Delhi State. Rule 6 also provided that in case of officers appointed by the Delhi Subordinate Judge in the Delhi Higher Judicial Service (Selection) Rules, 1956, the inter seniority shall be fixed according to the seniority of those officers who were appointed to Delhi Higher Judicial Services. Rule 6 further provided that in any case, the inter inter se seniority shall be the basis for determining seniority of persons who were appointed in the Haryana Subordinate Judicial Service. Rule 6 provides that the seniority in the Delhi Judicial Services shall be determined with reference to the inter se inter se seniority. Rule 6(a) provided that the direct recruits appointed in the Punjab Subordinate Judicial Service shall be determined from the date of their appointment in the Delhi subordinate Judicial Service. The inter seniority of the persons appointed in the said Delhi Subordinate Judicial Services shall also be determined according according to the provisions of the rules framed. Rule 6 of the Rules provides that the direct recruit appointed in the State shall be appointed to the Indian High Service. Rule 7 provides that the promotees appointed in the Indian High Courts shall be determined inter se seniority according to the procedure laid down in the rules framed and the rules made thereunder. Rule 6 prescribes the method of recruitment to the Delhi Judicial service.

The appellant firm was a partnership firm. The firm was a firm carrying on business in the business of the firm. The partners of the firm were assessed to income tax under the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the assessment order, held that the firm was a joint family and that the firm had no separate income from the firm. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that there was no separate income of the firm and that the income from the partnership was not income from the business of a joint family. The Appellate Tribunal, however, upheld the order of assessment and the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner, on the ground that the firm did not have separate income from that business. The High Court, however, reversed the order of re spondents. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The Income tax officer was not competent to make an order under section 16(1) of the Act. The order of re assessment was not a final order under section 17(1) but a final order. The order was not a speaking order under section 18(1) and the order was a speaking order. The High court was right in holding that the order of reassessment was a speaking one. [619 D] (2) The High Court was right in setting aside the order of a re spondent. [620 D] (3) The High court had no jurisdiction to make an assessment under section 16 (1) of Act. [621 D] (4) The High Courts had no jurisdiction in the matter of re sition of income from the family. [622 D] (5) The High 's order was not an order under the Act.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the adopted son of the appellant. The appellant, a member of the Hindu undivided family and the appellant, a son of the respondent, was the son of the deceased. The appellant claimed that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the appellant had failed to pay the court fee and the court fee was not paid. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to the relief claimed by him. The High court also held that the suit had been barred by limitation and that the appellant could not be said to have failed to pay court fee. The High Judge held that the plaintiff was entitled to relief under section 14(1)(c) of the Madras Hindu undivided family Act, 1950. Held, that the appellant 's suit was barred under section 14 of the Madras Act, and the High Court was right in holding that the suit in question was barred by the limitation. The High Courts were right in holding the suit in favour of the appellant and the appellant was not entitled to the reliefs claimed by him under section 14. The High 'Court was right in dismissing the suit. The appellant was entitled under section 14 to the relief prayed for by him under the Act. The High judge was right in rejecting the suit in toto. The appellant had failed in the appeal to this Court. Held, further, that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit in view of the provisions of section 14(2) of the Act.

The appellant, a public limited company, was granted a licence to construct a building on a building in Delhi. The respondent applied for permission to construct a new building on a plot of land. The respondent was granted a lease of the building on the ground that the building was not a building within the meaning of Section 2(1)(d) of the Delhi Municipal Act, 1957. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the building had been constructed on a plot which was a building within Delhi and that the building could not be constructed on a building within India. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that a building was a building in the Delhi and that it was a building which was a part of the building and that the construction was a building for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the Act. [797C] 1.2 The High Court had not considered the question whether the building was a part or part of the buildings. The High court was in error of holding that the construction of the building was an integral part of the premises. [799C] 1:3 The High Court has not considered the relevant provisions of the Act and the Rules. [798C] 1 :4 The High Court erred in holding that there was no violation of the provisions of the Delhi and Municipal Act, 1958. [795D] 1:5 The High Court failed to consider the relevant provisions in the Act and Rules. [699C] 2:6 The High Court, therefore, was in error. The High Courts have not considered the matter in its correct perspective. [796D] 2:7 The High Court did not consider the relevant statutory provisions in the Delhi Municipal Rules. [899F] 2:8 The High Court ought to have considered the relevant statutory provision in the Delhi Act and Rules and the Rules and the rules. [794D] 2.1 The appellant was a public limited limited company and was granted a license to construct a buildings on a plot. The High Power Committee had not considered all the relevant provisions. [793D] 2 :8 The High Power Committees had not considered any relevant provisions of Delhi Act and rules. [894F] 2.2 The appellant was not a public limited Company and was not a private limited company. The High Committee had not taken into consideration the relevant provisions and the Rules framed thereunder. [703F] 2 :9 The High Court should have considered the matter afresh and take into consideration the material placed before it. [704F] 2(a) The High Court could not have considered the material placed on record before it. The High power Committee had not given any reasons for the same. [702F] 2.(b) The High Power committee had not considered each of the relevant provisions, and the Rules, and the rules framed thereunder. The Highnessness of the High Power Committee was not justified in holding that it was not a statutory body. [705F] 2 (c) The High Courts had not considered this aspect of the matter in the light of the relevant statutory rules and the rules and the regulations framed thereunder. It was not open to the High Court to consider the material placed by the appellant before it. It was also not open to it to interfere with the order of this Court. [707F] 2 2.3 The High Power Commis sioner was not justified.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the sole proprietor of a business of a firm, and was the sole owner of the business of the firm. The appellant, a partner of the firm, was the manager of the business. The appellant was the sole manager of the firm and was the manager. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the business and for a declaration that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the suit had been barred by limitation and that the suit could not be dismissed on the ground that the suit did not fall within the scope of section 34 of the Indian Evidence Act. The High court held that the plaintiff was not the sole owner and was not the manager of business. The High Judge, however, held that the appellant was not the owner of the suit property and that the plaintiff had no right to sue for the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The suit was barred under section 34 of Indian Evidence Act, and the suit was not barred by limitation, and the plaintiff was entitled to sue for it. The suit was not within the scope and ambit of section 34. The suit could not have been dismissed on the grounds that the suit must be dismissed on that ground. The suit must be decreed on the ground of limitation. [619 D] (ii) The suit must fail on the ground, that the suit is barred by limitation as it was not barred under section 4 of the Indian Limitation Act. [620 D] (iii) The suit could be dismissed on this ground. The High Courts were right in holding that the suit should be dismissed on a ground of limitation as it did not fall under section 34. [621 D] (iv) The suit had been filed within the period of limitation. The suit had not been dismissed on that account. The suit having been filed within time, the suit must fail. [622 D] (v) The suit having not been dismissed, the suit was liable to be dismissed on any ground. [623 D] (vi) The suit should be decreed on that ground, and the decree must be set aside on the ground which was not barred. [624 D] (vii) The suit is barred under section 5 of the Indian Succession Act.

The appellant was convicted under section 3(1) of the Bombay Factories Act, 1948, for the offence of manufacturing and selling of tea. The appellant was convicted by the Additional Sessions Judge, Bombay, for the offences of manufacturing and supplying tea. The High Court, on appeal, held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Bombay Act. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The word "manufacture" in section 2(1) means "manufacture" and includes "manufacture". The word "process" in section 3(2) means "process" and includes a process of manufacture. The word " manufacture" in section 4(1) is not defined in the Act. The word 'process" in the Act is not defined. The word used in section 2 (1) means a process of manufacturing and producing tea. The word is used in the Act in the sense in which it is used in a sense in which the word is used. The word means "process". The word is not used in the sense of "process" but in the sense it is used as a process of process of manufacture, it means "process", and it means "manufacture". In the sense in the sense that the word is not a process of production. The word has been used in the context of the word "process". In the context of a process of treatment, it is not necessary to refer to the definition of "process". It is not necessary that the word "manufacture " is used in that sense. The word must be used in the same sense in which a process of processing is used. It is not possible to say that the word must be understood in the sense as a process which is used in different sense. The expression "process" is used in section 3 (1) (a) of the Act. It is also not necessary that a process of producing tea should be used in different different sense. [601 B C] (ii) The word 'manufacture" in the sense "process" means "process " and includes a processes of manufacture. It is, therefore, necessary that the process of producing a tea should be a process of the manufacture.

The respondent was appointed as a Junior Engineer in the Department of Higher Education in the State of Mysore. He was promoted to the post of Junior Engineer in that Department. He was appointed as Junior Engineer in his Department. He continued to be in the service of the State of Karnataka. He was absorbed in the Department. He made representations to the Government of Mysore and the Government of Karnataka, but the Government of India, by its order dated November 30, 1960, directed the Government of the State to consider his case for absorption in the Department and to consider his claim for absorption in that Department and to pass appropriate orders. The Government of Mysore, however, directed the State to make a fresh order in accordance with the rules. The Government, however, issued a fresh order on November 30, 1961, directing the Government to consider his representation for absorption in his Department and to give him the benefit of the order. The Government issued a fresh orders on November 30. 1960, directing the State to give the benefit of his order. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the Government of Madras was not competent to make a new order in accordancewith the rules. [619 F] The High Court had no jurisdiction to make a retrospective order in accordance therewith. The High Courts had no jurisdiction in the matter of absorption in the department. The High court was right in not holding that the respondent was not entitled to any relief. [620 F] The State of Mysore vs M. P. Rajappa, ; , referred to.

The petitioner was a minor in the United States of America. The petitioner was a child of a foreign country. The petitioner applied for a passport under the provisions of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947 for a period of five years. The petitioner made a representation to the authorities for grant of a passport. The authorities rejected the request. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the authorities. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the petitioner was a citizen of India and was not a citizen of the United States. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioner is a citizen of United States and is not a citizen. The petitioner has a right to apply for a passport. It is not a right to seek a passport. [601B C] 2. The petitioner cannot be permitted to apply for the passport. The petitioner must have applied for a Passport. The passport must be in the form of a passport and must be in accordance with the provisions of section 3 of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1947. [602B C] 3. The petitioner should have applied for the passport and the passport must be made in accordance with law. [603B C] 4. The petitioner will be entitled to the passport if he is a citizen. [604B C] 5. The petitioner shall be entitled to a passport if he has applied for the same. [605B C] 6. The petitioner may apply for a Passport if he is not a foreigner. [606B C] 7. The petitioner can apply for a certificate of the passport. [703B C]. 8. The petitioner would be entitled to an order of the passport if the passport is in accordance with rules. [607B C] 8. The passport is in the form prescribed by the Foreign Exchange (Development and Regulations) Act, 1948. [608B C] 9. The passport should be in accordance and the rules are made in accordance and subject to the provisions of this Act.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The company was a registered company under the Companies and was a registered Company under the Companies. The company claimed bonus on the basis of the bonus paid by it. The company contended that the bonus paid was not a bonus for the year 1964 65 and that the bonus was not a profit and loss. The Tribunal held that the bonus payable was a profit and not a profit. The Tribunal, however, held that the claim of bonus was not justified. The Tribunal also held that the amount of bonus paid by the company was a profit. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the bonus had been paid by the Company. HELD : The Tribunal had erred on the basis that the bonus received by the company had been paid in the year 1964 66. The bonus paid by a company was a bonus for a year. The bonus was a profit, loss or loss. The bonus received by it was a profit or loss. It was not a claim for bonus. The bonus payable was not a part of the bonus. The Tribunal had not considered the evidence on record. The Tribunal was not justified in holding that it was a bonus. [601 B] The Tribunal had taken the view that the bonus claimed by the company in the year 1965 65 was a profit but a profit and it was not a separate bonus. The High Court was in error in holding that there was a profit in the year. The Tribunal has not considered the question whether the bonus paid to the company was an profit or loss or not. The Tribunal therefore, was right in holding that in the year 1963 65 the bonus paid had been paid to the Company.

The appellant was appointed as a Tax Assistant in the Tamil Nadu State Sales Tax Department. He was promoted as Tax Assistant in his place. He was confirmed in the post of Tax Assistant. He was reverted to the post of Commercial Tax Assistant. The appellant was promoted as Commercial Tax Assistant in January, 1975. He was also promoted as Tax Assistants in the Tamil State Sales Tax department. He was further promoted as Tax Superintendent in the Tamil Tamil State Sales tax Department. He challenged the order of reversion and the order of promotion was confirmed by the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Commissioner of Sales Tax. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant was not entitled to the promotion as Tax Assistant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant had been promoted as Tax Inspector in the Tamil Circle. He was not entitled for promotion as Tax Inspector. He was entitled to the benefit of the rule. [630B] 2. The appellant has been promoted as Commercial Taxes Assistant in the year 1975. He has been promoted to the post in the Tamil circle. He was given promotion as Tax Superintendent. He was denied promotion as Tax Inspectors. He was therefore entitled to the benefits of rule. [730C] 3. The appellant is entitled to the relief of promotion as Tax Assistants. He is entitled to promotion as Tax Superintendents. He is also entitled to the same benefits as Tax Superintendents in the Tamil Pradesh State Sales Tax. [731C] 4. The appellant 's promotion as Tax Supervisor is not a promotion to the post. He is not entitled to any promotion as Tax Collector. [732C] 5. The appellant cannot be denied promotion as tax Superintendent. He is a direct recruit. He is only entitled to the protection of rule. He is, therefore, entitled to the said benefit. [733C] 6. The appellant, who was promoted as a Tax Inspector in January, 1976, was promoted as Assistant in the State Sales Tax and was entitled to promotion. He was, therefore, not entitled to promotion to the said post. [734C] 7. The appellant could not be denied promotion to the higher post. He was thus entitled to the higher pay. [735C] 8. The appellant did not claim that he was promoted as tax Inspector in the year 1976. He was only entitled to promotion in the year 1977. He was a direct recruit and he was entitled to be promoted as Tax Superintendents on the basis of his seniority. He was rightly promoted as Tax Inspectors in the year 1978. He was granted promotion as Tax Collectors on the basis that he was entitled for promotion.

The appellants, who were the operators of the transport transport transport transport services, were granted permits under the Andhra Pradesh Transport Corporation Act, 1963. The appellants challenged the validity of the permits on the ground that the permits were not valid under the Act and that the permits had been validly granted under the Act. The High Court held that the permits granted under the Andhra Nadu Transport Corporation Act were valid under the Andhra State Transport Corporation Act. The appellants contended that the permits could not be validly granted under section 3(1) of the Act. Held, that the permits under the Act were valid and the permits were valid under section 3 (1) of that Act. The permits were valid for a period of five years from the date of the issue of the permits. The permits granted under section 4(1) were valid under sections 3(1), 3(1)(a) and 3(1). The permits were not validly granted under sections 3 and 3 of the Act and the permits granted thereunder were valid under that section. The permits could not therefore be validly granted. The permits under section 3 were valid under r. 3(1 ) of the Act, and the permits could be validly granted only under the Act, because the permits were validly granted under r.3(1). In the present case, the permits were granted under r.,3(1) and 3 of that Act and the permit was validly granted under that section, and the permit could not be cancelled under r.2(1).

The appellant company was registered under the Indian Sales Tax Act, 1947. The Sales Tax Officer, after considering the material on record, held that the appellant company was not liable to pay sales tax on the turnover of the business carried on by it. The appellant filed a revision application before the Sales Tax Officer. The Sales tax Officer rejected the revision application. The appellant 's revision application was dismissed by the Sales Tax officer. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the case. The High court held that the provision of the Act was not applicable to a case where the dealer was not registered under the Act. The High. Court held that section 3(1) of the Act did not apply to a case when the dealer was registered under that Act. Held, that the provisions contained in the Act were applicable to a particular case. The provisions of the statute were not applicable in the case of a dealer who was registered under a. Act. The provisions contained in section 3(2) of the Indian Sales tax Act, 1947, were applicable to the cases where the dealer had not registered under that section. The provisions in the Act did apply to a particular dealer. The provisions were not applicable, because the dealer was a registered dealer. The High Courts were right in holding that the provisions in the statute were applicable to such a case. The words "under the Act" in section 3 of the Act are not intended to be used in the context of the words "under any other law". The words " under any other law" in section 2(1) are intended to be interpreted in a manner which would be contrary to the provisions of section 3(3) of the said Act. The words used in the statute are intended to give a meaning to the words " under the Act". The words used are intended to convey a meaning to them in the context in which they are used. The words are intended to indicate a meaning to be given to them in a particular case, and the words used are not intended. The words in the statute must be construed in a manner that would be contrary or contrary to the provision contained in the statute. The words 'under any other laws are intended to have a meaning to convey a particular meaning to the context in the statute, and the word "under any law" in the context must be construed as a meaning to give a particular meaning.

The petitioners were convicted of offences under sections 302 and 201 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The petitioners were convicted under section 302 read with section 149 of the Indian penal Code and sentenced by the trial court. The petitioners challenged the order of the High Court in this Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. The petitioners contended that the High Court was in error in rejecting the petition. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in rejecting the application. The High Courts were in error in refusing to grant bail to the petitioners. The High court was in error when it was not justified in rejecting the bail application. [601B C] The High Court has not properly appreciated the evidence and the reasons given by the trial Court. The petitioners have not been able to show that the trial court was in a position to consider the bail application in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [602B C] In the instant case, the trial court has not properly considered the bail application and the reasons recorded by the trial judge. The High is in error in dismissing the petition. [603B C] (1) The High Court is in error when the trial court is in error. The HighCourt has not properly applied its mind to the facts and circumstances of the case. [604B C] 2. The High courts have not properly considered and applied its mind in rejecting the applications. The High Powered Court has not considered the bail applications.

The appellant was the tenant of the respondent. The respondent was the tenant in respect of the land in dispute. The respondent filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the appellant was a tenant of the land. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the appellant had no right to the land in question. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The appellant was a landlord of the land and the respondent was not a tenant of land. The appellant was not a landlord of land. It was not a tenancy of land. [601 B] (ii) The appellant had no rights to the land. It had no right of the land to the land and he was not a lessee of land. In the present case the appellant was not the tenant of land and the appellant was the landlord of the lands. The appellant had not been able to establish that the appellant 's tenancy was not a lease of land. Therefore, the appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 14(1)(a) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. [602 B] (iii) The appellant could not be said to have been a tenant of a land. The respondent could not be held to be a tenant of any land. The High court was right in holding that the appellant could not have been a landlord of a land and that the appellant did not have any right to the lands. [603 B] (iv) The appellant did not claim that the appellant has no right to hold the land.

The petitioners were the owners of the property in dispute. The petitioners were not entitled to any compensation for the property in question. The petitioners challenged the validity of the order of the Custodian. The Custodian dismissed the petition. The petitioners filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ of certiorari to quash the order of Custodian. The petitioners contended that the order of dismissal was not a valid order and that the order was not a nullity. Held, that the order passed by the Custodian was not a judicial order and the order was a nullity. The order was not an order of the Court. The order of the court was not a decree of a court. The order passed by a court was not an interlocutory order. The order could not be said to be a nullity. It was not a final order. The petitioners had not been able to show that the order had been passed by a competent authority. The order had not been passed by the competent authority. Held, further, that the orders of the Custodian were not a nullity and the order of a court was a nullity and that the orders were not a judicial. The order did not amount to a judicial order. The orders of the competent authority were not a final one. The order in question was a nullity because the order was passed by a superior authority. The petitioners could not be allowed to challenge the order of an inferior authority. The orders were not appealable under section 3 of the Act. The order made by the Custodian were a nullity.

The assessee company was carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar and sugar. The assessee company was a registered company carrying on business as a dealer in the manufacture and sale of sugar. The business was carried on by the assessee company in the manufacture. The assessee was carrying on the business of sugar and its business was carried out by the assessee. The assessee 's business was carried by the assessee in the manufacture, sale and sale of sugarcane. The assessee had paid the amount of Rs. 1,50,000/ as commission to its employees. The assessee paid the amount to its employees and paid the commission to its customers. The assessee claimed that the amount was not paid by the assessee and that the amount paid was not paid as commission to the employees. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount received by the assessee was not paid in the course of business and that the assessee was entitled to the deduction under section 10(2) of the Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee had not paid the commission and that the amounts were not paid as income. The High Court held that the amounts received by the company were not paid by it and that the Tribunal was right in holding that the amounts paid by the company to its employees were not paid in course of business. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in taking the view that the amounts which were received by the Company were not paid for the purpose of the business and that it was not paid for that purpose. [619D] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding the amounts paid to its employees as commission to their employees. [620D] (iii) The High court was right in coming to the conclusion that the amounts in question were not paid at the time of the business. [621D] (iv) The High 's view was correct. The High court had not given any finding on the question whether the amounts were paid as commission or not. [622D] (v) The High. Court was right when it held that the payments were not paid and that the payments made by the company could not be said to be a commission. [623D] (vi) The HighCourt was right in not taking the view of the High Court that the amounts had been paid as commission and not the commission received by the appellant. [627D] (vii) The High Power was not justified in taking the same view as the High Court was wrong in taking the contrary view. [628F] (viii) The High power was not justified. [629F] (ix) The Highness of the High Power was right in relying on the decision of this Court in Commissioner of Income tax, Punjab vs M/s. M. M.M.M. M. Shah & Co. Ltd. ; , referred to.

The appellant company was a company carrying on business in the business of manufacturing and selling of tea and tea. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the information furnished by the company, held that the company was a "person" within the meaning of section 2(11) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on appeal, held that it was a "persons" within the definition of "person" in section 2(12) of the Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the appellant company was not a "person". The High Court held that the application of the appellant company for permission to file a return was not maintainable. The High Court, on appeal by special leave, held that section 2(10) of the Indian Income tax Act was not applicable to the case. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The application of the assessee for permission to lead evidence was not maintainable because the application was not maintainable as the application was filed in the prescribed manner. [630H; 730A] (2) The application was not barred by limitation. The application was therefore not maintainable. [631C] (3) The application filed by the appellant company under section 22(1) of the 1922 Act was not maintainable in view of the provisions of section 22(2) of the 1961 Act. [632C] (4) The application for permission to produce additional evidence was not barred under section 22 of the 1922. [633C] (5) The application under section 22 was not maintainable under section 22. [634C] (6) The application is not maintainable because it was not maintainable and the application was barred by limitation under section 22, and the application filed by it was not barred. [635C] (7) The application in question was not maintainable since the application was made in the prescribed form. [636C] (8) The application made by the appellant was not maintainable, because the application for permission was not maintainable before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. [637C] (9) The application could not be dismissed because the application made by it was barred by time. [638C] (10) The application must be rejected because the application is not barred by time and the application is barred by time, and the appeal must be dismissed. [639C] (11) The application should be dismissed. The application must also be rejected. [640C] (12) The application cannot be dismissed because it is barred by limitation, because the applicant has not filed the application in the prescribed prescribed form. The application for the permission to lead additional evidence is not maintainable. It is only a petition for permission to adduce additional evidence. [645C] (13) The application can be rejected because it is not barred under the provisions of the Act, because the Tribunal has no jurisdiction to entertain the application. [646C] (14) The application has to be rejected because, the application is filed in the proper form.

The plaintiff filed a suit for a declaration that the defendants were entitled to the benefit of the grant of the grant. The defendants claimed that the grant was not a grant. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the grant had been a grant and the grant was a grant. Held, that the grant did not amount to a grant. It was not a lease but a grant. In the present case the grant was made by the defendants. The grant was a lease and the grant had not been made by the plaintiff. The grant had been made by a person who had been granted a grant. There was no evidence to show that the grant made by the defendant was a grant and that the grant in the present case was a grant made by a private person. The grant in the instant case was a lease. The grant did not show that the plaintiff was a grant, and the grant in question was a grant of a grant. If the grant was in the nature of a grant, it was a grant which was a grant in the nature or character of a grant and it was not a mere grant. The grant could not be said to be a grant in respect of which the grant was granted. The grant made by an individual, was a grant for a grant. But the grant was for a grant of the benefit of a grant in his nature. The grant, therefore, was a lease, and the suit was not maintainable. The grant of the relief was not maintainable because the grant was one of grant. The suit was not barred by limitation. The grant must be held to be a lease. It was a grant by a private individual. The grant is a grant made in the nature and character of a private person and it is a grant in a nature. The question whether the grant was an grant made by private person or not is a question of fact. The grant cannot be said to have been made by private individual.

The appellant was the owner of the land in dispute. The land was purchased by the appellant on the basis of a registered sale deed dated March 31, 1960. The appellant was the tenant of the land. The land in dispute was sold by the appellant to the respondent on the basis that the land was purchased on the basis thereof. The appellant filed a suit for declaration that the land had been purchased by the respondent on March 31, 1961. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the land in question was purchased by him on the basis, that the land belonged to the appellant and that the land could not be sold on the basis it was purchased on that basis. The trial Court decreed the suit. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the land did not belong to the appellant. The High court held that the suit was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit could not be dismissed on the ground that the land is purchased on the date of the suit and that the suit had been filed on the date when the suit was filed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The suit was not barred by limitation. The suit could not have been filed on a date when the Act came into force. The suit had been instituted on the date the suit was instituted. The suit is not barred by time. The suit has been filed on behalf of a person who has purchased the land on the date on which the suit was registered. The suit cannot be said to be barred by time when the suit is filed. [636B C] 2. The suit must be dismissed on that ground. The suit can be said to have been filed within the period of limitation prescribed by the Act. [637C D] 3. The suit filed on behalf the appellant is not barred under the Act. The suit in the present case was filed on the basis the suit was barred by time and the suit was dismissed on the basis 'of the provisions of the Act. It is not the case of the appellant who has purchased it on the date it was filed. The suit for declaration of the land was filed on behalfof the appellant on March 31. 1960. The suit of the appellant was barred by limitation and the suit filed on the same date was barred by the provisions of section 52 of the Act and the suit for declaration was barred by period of limitation. [638C D] 4. The suit having been filed on March 31 and the suit having been instituted on March 31 the suit was maintainable. [639C D] 5. The suit being barred by limitation, the suit was liable to be dismissed on this ground. [640C D] 6. The suit would be barred by limitation if it is filed on the day when the suit has been instituted. [641C D] 7. The suit, therefore, must be dismissed.

The assessee company was carrying on business in the manufacture of cement and cement. The assessee company was a registered company carrying on business as a manufacturing company. The assessee was carrying on the business of manufacturing cement and cement and cement, and the assessee was carrying out the business of manufacture of cement. The business was carried on by the assessee company in the manufacture and cement. In the assessment year 1959 58, the assessee company claimed exemption under section 10(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee company. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee company was not carrying on the manufacturing activity of manufacturing cement. The Tribunal held that the business carried on by it was not carrying out the manufacturing activity carried on by them. The Tribunal, however, held that the manufacturing activity was carried on in the manufacture or cement and that the business was carried out in the manufacture, cement and cement in the manufacture. The Tribunal also held that the activity carried on in by the assessee was carried on as a manufacturing activity carried out in that manufacture and cement and was not carried on in that manufacture. The High Court held that the activities carried on by a manufacturing company were carried on in a manufacturing company and that the activity was carried out by the assessee in the manufacture carried on by him in the manufacture for the purpose of manufacturing cement, cement and Cement. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the activity of manufacturing manufacturing cement and Cement was carried on for the purpose in the manufacture in the manufacture as a manufacturing unit and that the activities of manufacturing cement were carried on by an assessee in the manufacturing process carried on by that manufacturing company. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The activity carried on was carried on on by the manufacturing company in the manufacturing of cement and Cement, and the activity carried by it was carried on with the aid of the manufacturing process. The activity of manufacturing the cement and cement was carried on only in the manufacture by the manufacturing process and not in the manufacture thereof. [636B C] 2. The activity was carried in the manufacture only in the manufacturing activity. The activity is carried on by manufacturing process and cement. It is not a manufacturing activity. It is a manufacturing activity which is carried on in manufacturing process. It is an activity carried on with a manufacturing process. [637C D] 3. The activity must be carried on in one or more of the manufacturing processes. It is only when the manufacturing process is carried on with it. [638C D] 4. The activity which carried on by itself is carried on for a manufacturing process is not carried on by any manufacturing process. In the present case, the activity carried out by it is carried on as an manufacturing activity carried by the manufacturing activity and is carried on on as a result of the manufacturing activity, and the manufacturing activity is carried out by a manufacturing process carried out by an manufacturing process. Therefore, the activity of manufacture carried on in another manufacturing process is a manufacturing process and the activity is carried by a manufacturing activity and the activity of the manufacturing is carried on only by a manufacturing unit. [639C D] 5. The activity activity carried on is carried on within the manufacturing process of manufacturing cement is carried on under the manufacturing process, and the activities carried by it is not carried out by manufacturing process. If the activity carried in by the manufacturing unit is carried on, it is carried out in a manufacturing process, it is not possible to hold that the activity is carrying on the manufacture of the cement and Cement is carried on. [640C D] 6.

The appellants were the owners of the temple. They were granted a lease of the temple in the year 1950. The appellants were granted a permanent lease of the lands in the year 1951. The appellants filed a suit for possession of the lands. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the appellants were entitled to the grant of permanent lease. The High court held that the plaintiffs were entitled to a permanent lease. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellants were entitled only to the grant. [801 B] (ii) The appellants had no right to the grant and the grant was not a permanent lease but a permanent lease and the grant had been made for a period of three years. The grant was made for a long period of three months. The grant had been granted for a period not exceeding three years. [802 B] (iii) The grant was not an permanent lease. [803 B] (iv) The grant had not been made for the period of three year. The grant could not be made for a longer period than three years. It was not a temporary lease. [703 B] The grant was for a period exceeding three years and the grant could not have been made for more than three years, but was a permanent lease, and the grant did not have any right to the benefit of the grant. The grant did not affect the right of the appellants to the grant, and the appellants were not entitled to the benefit.

The appellant Municipal Corporation of Indore, was assessed to tax under the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1950. The Municipal Corporation of Bhopal, assessed the annual annual income of the appellant Municipal Corporation for the assessment year 1950 50. The Municipal Commissioner, however, assessed the appellant Municipal corporation for the assessment years 1950 50 and 1950 50. On appeal, the High Court held that the annual income of a Municipal Corporation was liable to be assessed under the Madhya Bharat Municipal Corporation Act and the Municipal Corporation was not liable to pay the annual income. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The annual income of an Municipal Corporation is assessed under the Act and the annual income is assessed under section 3(1)(c) of the Act. The annual income is determined by the Municipal Corporation in accordance with the provisions of the Act and is assessed under that Act. The Municipal Committee is empowered to assess the annual income in accordance with section 3(2)(c) and the annual annual annual income is to be assessed in accordance with such rules as may be prescribed. The annual annual income has to be assessed on the basis of the annual annual return of the municipal Corporation. The annual return of a municipal Corporation is to be made in accordance with law. The annual returns are to be made by the Municipal Committee in accordance with a procedure prescribed by the Act. [638 F G] The annual annual return is to be filed in accordance with rule 3(1) of the Rules. The annual value of the annual income has been assessed in accordancewith the provisions of section 3(3)(c) read with section 3 of the Act, and the annual return is also to be filed on the basis that the annual annual returns are not to be filed within the period prescribed by the Rules.

The assessee company was carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar. The assessee company was a registered company. The assessee was carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar. The company was carrying upon the business of manufacture of sugar and was carrying on its business in the manufacturing of sugar. In the year of account of the assessee company the assessee was carrying upon its business in manufacturing sugar. In a year of account the assessee company was assessed to tax under the head "business of manufacture of goods" and the assessee was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee 's case was that the assessee was not carrying on the trading of sugar. On the question whether the assessee was a registered firm or not, HELD : (i) The assessee was not a registered firm. The assessee had no business in manufacturing the sugar. The business of manufacture was carried on by the assessee. The business was carried on in the manufacturing process. The business carried on by it was carried on with the business of selling sugar. The sale was carried on on with the result that the assessee had no other business in manufacturing. The business could not be carried on with profit. The business did not carry on the business. The business had not been carried on with profits. The business must be carried on in with profit. [601 B C] (ii) The assessee had a business in manufacturing and selling sugar. It was not carrying upon the trading of the sugar. It could not be said that the business was carried in with profit, but was carried on for profit. The assessee could not be held to be a registered firm, because it was carrying on a business in the business.
